kanji/上.title: 上
kanji/上.content:
上

Above, Up


On: ジョウ, ショウ, シャン
Kun: うえ, -うえ, うわ-, かみ, あ.げる, -あ.げる, あ.がる, -あ.がる, あ.がり, -あ.がり, のぼ.る, のぼ.り, のぼ.せる, のぼ.す, たてまつ.る
Kyūjitai: 丄
Componentes: ⺊, 一


Etimología
From zh sit-pro *tVŋ  top. Cognate with bo སྟེང, bo ཡང་རྩེ  summit; pinnacle (Bodman, 1980), lus zo  to be high, lus zah  to respect; to revere (STEDT).  | Shijing rimes indicate occasional level tone for pronunciation 2 (Schuessler, 2007). | Pronunciation 1 is the exopassive of pronunciation 2 with suffix *-s, literally meaning “what has been raised” (Schuessler, 2007). The rising tone in Middle Chinese words with voiced stop initials regularly evolves into departing tone in Mandarin. Pronunciation 3 results from 叶韻, i.e. its pronunciation has been artificially changed to preserve rhymes in classical poetry.

kanji/下.title: 下
kanji/下.content:
下

Below, Down, Descend, Give, Low, Inferior


On: カ, ゲ
Kun: した, しも, もと, さ.げる, さ.がる, くだ.る, くだ.り, くだ.す, -くだ.す, くだ.さる, お.ろす, お.りる
Kyūjitai: 丅
Componentes: 一, 卜


Etimología
zh :der sit-pro:*(k/g)la-k/j/t | From zh sit-pro *(k/g)la-k/j/t  to fall (STEDT): | * inside Sinitic, cognate with 落 to fall, to drop, 露 dew, 陊 to collapse and 阤 hillside, slope; | * outside Sinitic, cognate with lus tla ~ tlâk  to fall, lus thla ~ thlâk  to drop, my ကျ  to fall and my ချ  to drop. | Schuessler (2007) instead proposed an zh aav origin by comparing 下 to descend, down, below to km; additionally, he suggested that Sino-Tibetan influence had possibly caused the weakening of foreign final *-k to OC final *-ʔ. kanji/不.title: 不
kanji/不.content:
不

Negative, Non-, Bad, Ugly, Clumsy


On: フ, ブ
Kun: —
Kyūjitai: 㐬
Componentes: 一


Etimología
Old Chinese had two sets of negatives: the initial *p-series and the initial *m-series. zh 不 is the prototype of the *p-series of negatives. Although it is the usual Literary Chinese negative attested from the oracle bone script down, its current usage is now confined to Mandarin dialects. In the oracle bone inscriptions, a total of five negative particles can be found: *不, *弗, *毋, *勿 and *非. With the exception of *非 (discussed later), the remaining can be neatly organised into the following system: | {| class=“wikitable” style=“text-align:center” | ! !! *-V !! *-ɯd | |- | ! *p-type negatives ((無) || 勿 | |} | Takashima (1996) argued that the *m-type negatives are modal (i.e. negative verbs which are thought of as controllable by the Shang Dynasty Shang), whereas the *p-type negatives are non-modal (imply uncontrollability; actions which are beyond the control of living persons). | In the p-series, zh 不 usually goes with intransitive verbs in the oracle bone script, and 弗 with transitive ones, although there are some glaring exceptions. Little or no pattern can be discerned in the m-type category. Takashima (1996) also proposed that the difference between the two vowel series was whether they preceded “stative, eventive, passive” (-V series) or “non-stative, non-eventive, active” (-ɯd series) verbs. | It is possible that the two parallel series of negatives in Old Chinese represent a fusion of the common Sino–Tibetan sit-pro *ma  no, not (carried by the eastward-migrating early Sino–Tibetans) and an indigenous negation system in Central China, and that the merger had been complete by the Shang Dynasty Shang times. Compare a similar system in Proto-Tai: tai-pro *ɓawᴮ  not [strong form 1], tai-pro *boːᴮ  not [strong form 2], tai-pro *miːᴬ  not [weak form]; th บ่  (literary, archaic, dialectal) not. | The development from Old Chinese to Middle Chinese was not regular. The character zh 不 replaced zh 弗 (OC *pɯd, MC *piut), to respect the naming taboo for Emperor Zhao of Han, although the pronunciation has remained in nearly all topolects (e.g. Beijing Mandarin bù, Guangzhou Cantonese bat1, Meixian Hakka bud5, Shanghainese Wu peq). The Modern Standard Mandarin pronunciation is also from this checked coda word, but this word escaped from regular sound changes during its evolution to the modern pronunciation bù. The expected reading is fu (tone undetermined), with labiodentalisation. The rising-tone pronunciation had a Middle Chinese homophone *否 not, which is now primarily used in compounds, and demonstrates the regular development into modern f-. Another example of a high-frequency word escaping this sound change is 父 dad, which resulted in the late coinage of the character 爸. | zh 不 is cognate with other negation particles in the *p-type category: | * 弗 not; | * 非 not be; not – can be safely regarded as a fusion of 不 not and 惟 to be; | * 否 not; to be wrong; | * 匪 it is not; to be not; and | * 棐 it is not; to be not. | Cognate with th บ่  (literary, archaic, dialectal) not (Schuessler, 2007).

Complete, Finish


On: リョウ

Componentes: 乛, 亅


Etimología
Verb “to finish; to be completed” > perfective aspect particle (zh 了₁, weakened form) > change-of-state modal particle (zh 了₂). It eventually replaced classical 矣.  | Two kinds of particle uses of zh 了 can be distinguished: the perfective aspect particle after verbs (conventionally written as zh 了₁) and the sentence-final modal particle (zh 了₂). It is generally accepted (Wu, 1998) that these two uses of zh 了 are derived from the concrete verb “to finish”. The grammaticalisation of this verb had become common in the Tang Dynasty, initially in the form of ‹verb + (object) + perfective zh 了› to indicate the completion of an action. | The perfective particle subsequently underwent further grammaticalisation to become the sentence-final change-of-state modal particle; Liu (1985) has demonstrated that this last step may have involved the coalescence of sentence-final zh 了 with *也 in certain Mandarin dialects, as the pronunciations of zh 了₁ and zh 了₂ are distinct in these dialects, with zh 了₂ rhyming with zh 也. | Contrary to the suggestion in Schuessler (2007), this word is not related to vi rồi, due to the non-existent correspondence between any given phonemes. th แล้ว  to be finished; already; then, afterwards, lo ແລ້ວ  to finish; to be completed; perfective particle are loans from Chinese.

kanji/令.title: 令
kanji/令.content:
令

On: レイ
Kun: —
Kyūjitai: 炩
Componentes: 亽, 龴


Etimología
Usually thought to be related to 命 order (Schuessler, 2007). Phonologically, the Old Chinese rhyme of this word shifted from the zhen (zh 真) group to the geng (zh 耕) group by the mid-Spring and Autumn period. | In Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, its orthography was strictly differentiated by context: *𪟹 was used as an adverb meaning “long-lasting” (*永), while *霝 was used specifically in the phrase *令終 good end. The common literary meaning “good; beautiful” (*善) likely evolved from this earlier sense of “long-lasting”.  | Furthermore, the sense of “season” (e.g., *時令) may derive directly from “rule; regular order”, rather than being an extension of “monthly ordinances” (*月令). During the Warring States period, the sense of “local magistrate” was often written as *命 or other variants (e.g., *𠊈, *𬔣) in Chu and Jin scripts. | As a surname, zh 令 has multiple origins, one being a shortened form of 令狐.

The semantics may have developed along the grammaticalisation process “bamboo stalk” (*箇) > “piece, item” > “classifier for every category of noun” > “possessive particle, generic particle”. If so, it would then possibly be cognate with 竿 bamboo, rod. Compare bo མཁར་བ, bo འཁར་བ  walking stick, staff and th ก้าน  stem, stalk. | ; Southern Min classifier and possessive particle | : Hokkien ê/gê (classifier), ê (possessive particle), Teochew gai5 (classifier), gai7 (possessive particle): from 其 (Li, 2002; Douglas, 1873). Cognate with cdo 其, mnp 的. The modern forms of these cognates all derive from the 陽平 tone. | ; Wu classifier and possessive particle | : Though the expected pronunciation (in for instance Shanghainese) would be /ku/, this has undergone glottalisation (Dai, 2004). Compare *勒 to be in, to be at, *搭 to. In Shanghainese, this often undergoes further lenition to /ɦəʔ/.

kanji/偽.title: 偽
kanji/偽.content:

Falsehood, Lie, Deceive, Pretend, Counterfeit, Forgery


On: ギ, カ
Kun: いつわ.る, にせ, いつわ.り
Kyūjitai: 僞
Componentes: 亻, 為


Etimología
Often thought to be derived from 為 to act as (Karlgren, 1956; Wang, 1982; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). | Alternatively, it may be cognate to 訛 erroneous (Schuessler, 2007); this may be compared to bo རྔོད  to deceive, though the -d in Tibetan is unexplained (Gong, 1995; Schuessler, 2007; Hill, 2014). | Jacques (2022, 2023) seems to attempt to unify the two etymologies above. He argues the ltc - initial ng- in both 偽 and 訛 come from a middle voice/intransitivizing prefix und *ŋ-. zh 偽, reconstructed as und *ŋ-waj-s, would be derived from 為 as the root.

kanji/儂.title: 儂
kanji/儂.content:
儂

I, My, He, His, Me (used By Old People)


On: ドウ, ノウ
Kun: わし, かれ
Kyūjitai: 人
Componentes: 亻, 農


Etimología
; “Person; I; me > suffix for pronouns” in southeastern varieties | Its senses of “person; human being” and “pronoun suffix” are well-attested in the classical literature, dating back to the Six Dynasties. At the present time, traces of this word are found in various Southern regions such as Fujian, Jiangxi and Zhejiang, in Wu, Min, Hui and Gan. | ; “Person; human” | : In Coastal Min (Eastern Min Eastern, Southern Min Southern and Puxian Min), it serves as the vernacular reading of 人 person, by itself or in compounds. It is also used in Jinqu Wu lects (also classified as Wuzhou Wu and Chuqu Wu), usually written as *農. | ; “I” | : zh 儂 was used to mean “I” in medieval poetry from the Wu region, before it was displaced by the more common 我 I. Also attested was Ancient Wu 阿儂 I, which was abbreviated to *阿 I in certain localities, such as that of Jinhua. | ; “Pronoun suffix” | : This is widely found in Wu and Min languages. The structure ‹ singular pronoun (“I, you, he/she/it”) + zh 儂 › is common, with zh 儂 functioning either as a meaningless particle or a pluraliser. The resulting forms were thus used to mean singular or plural pronouns, and were rather prone to elision to become a single syllable. Compare the following plural pronouns in Min: | : {| class=“wikitable” style=“text-align:center” | |- | ! Original word !! Meaning !! Fuding(Eastern Min)!! Longyan(Southern Min)!! Xiamen(Southern Min) !! Xianyou(Puxian Min) | |- | ! *我儂 !! we | | ua neiŋ || gua laŋ || gun (*阮) || kuoŋ ~ kŋ (*滾) | |- | ! *儂儂 !! we (inclusive) | | - || laŋ laŋ || lan (*咱) || - | |- | ! *汝儂 !! you (plural) | | ni neiŋ || li laŋ || lin (*恁) || tyøŋ (*長) | |- | ! *伊儂 !! they | | i neiŋ || i laŋ || in (*𪜶) || yøŋ (*𪜶) | |} | : A similar chain of changes happened in the Wu varieties to arrive at the modern divergent dialectal forms for “you (singular)”. | : {| class=“wikitable” style=“text-align:center” | |- | ! colspan=4 | 爾儂 | |- | ! colspan=2 | Lect !! colspan=2 | Term | |- | | rowspan=7 | Northern || Fenghua || /n̩˧˨˦ noŋ/ || 爾儂 | |- | | Yuyao || /noŋ˩˩˧/ || 儂 | |- | | Shanghai || /noŋ˩˩˧/ || 儂 | |- | | Ningbo || /nəu˨˩˧/ || 諾 | |- | | Changshu || /nɛ̃˧˩/ || 倷 | |- | | Suzhou|| /ne̞˧˩/ || 倷 | |- | | Shengze || /nə˧˩/ || 倷 | |- | | rowspan=2 | Jinqu || Tangxi || /ŋ˨˩˩ noŋ˩˨/ || 爾儂 | |- | | Lanxi || /ŋ˥˦˦ noŋ˦˧˧/ || 爾儂 | |} | : Some lects, such as Shanghainese, have merged the two syllables into one, leaving 儂 to mean “you (singular)”. | With regard to the etymology of this word, Huang (1980), Norman (1983) and Zhou (1986) hypothesised that this is the same as 農 farmer; peasant. The use of this word as a pronoun may have originated as a form of personal deprecation and then come to be used as a full-fledged pronoun. Pan and Chen (1995) disagree, proposing that nong was originally a Baiyue substrate word possibly of zh qfa-tak origin, and possibly an original clan name later developing to mean “person; I”. Compare za Nungz and name of the 11th century Zhuang leader Nong Zhigao, as well as the name of the Nùng people in Vietnam.

Beginning, Former Time, Origin


On: ゲン, ガン

Kyūjitai: 圓
Componentes: 一, 兀


Etimología
Possibly from sit-pro *m/s-gaw  head, with a noun-forming suffix *-n (Schuessler, 2003; STEDT). If so, cognate with 后, bo མགོ  head; summit; beginning, bo མགོན  protector; master; lord, grt sko  skull, tji kho⁵⁵ pa⁵⁵  head (Schuessler, 2007; STEDT). 原 and 黿 may be the same word (Schuessler, 2007). It may also be related to 君, 尹, 侯 (Mei, 1985). Possibly related to 圓. | The name of the dynasty comes from the I Ching: | : {{zh-x|大 哉 乾{qián} 元，萬物 資 始，乃 統 天。|Vast is the ‘great and originating (power)’ indicated by Qian! All things owe to it their beginning: - it contains all the meaning belonging to (the name) heaven.|ref=Yijing-L|collapsed=y}} | Part of the people with this surname are Xianbei descendants. It was changed from 拓跋 as ordered by Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei.

The irregular sound change is for taboo reasons - to avoid homophony with its derived vulgar meaning “to enter > to have sexual intercourse”, nowadays represented by 日.

But virtually all Old Chinese reconstructions of this word nowadays are completely phonetically incompatible with this etymon; this comparison should be rejected.  | Alternatively, Sagart (1999) and Baxter and Sagart (2014) suggest that this word is related to other words that express extraction, such as 掘 to dig out, and reconstruct the och - with an intransitivizing prefix *t-.

On the other hand, Sagart and Baxter (2012) consider the intransitive sense to be derived from the transitive sense (*pret) by prefixation of *N-, resulting in a voicing effect: *N-p- > *N-b- > *b-; compare 敗 to suffer defeat from 敗 to defeat.

劃

Divide


On: カク
Kun: わ.かつ, かぎ.る
Kyūjitai: 劃
Componentes: 畫, 刂


Etimología
Schuessler (2007) thinks the two verbs 畫 *ɡʷˤrek}} and 劃 *ɡʷˤrek also}} are related. Further, he proposes zh aav origin by comparing them to okz gvar gur ~ gvar to draw a line, to make a drawing and surmising that AA *gwer, when suffixed by OCh. *-k, became OCh. *gwrek due to: | * metathesis of *-r before *-k (also seen in 白 *bˤrak}} from *-k suffixed to Proto-Sino-Tibetan sit-pro *bar, whence also 皤 *[b]ˤar}} (ibid.)), and  | * vowel alternation between /*a/ and /*e ~ i/ (also seen in 良 *[r]aŋ}} & 令 *riŋ}}, 涼 *C.raŋ}} & 冷 *[r]ˤeŋʔ}}, etc.).

On: ケン
Kun: つるぎ
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 僉, 刂


Etimología
Schuessler (2007) minimally reconstructs 劍 *kams}} and proposes a possible native origin, from *k-nominalized adjective 剡 *jamʔ}}, which is from zh sit-pro *s-rjam  sharp and lost its *r- initial due to folk etymology; doublets 磏 whetstone and 鐮 sickle retain *r-. | Alternatively, the double-edged sword seemingly originated from the Nanman southern state of Wu (state) Wu (*吳); so a native Wu term, of unknown linguistic affiliation, might have yielded both och - 劍 and mkh-vie-pro *t-kɨəm ( > vi gươm).

kanji/北.title: 北
kanji/北.content:
北

North


On: ホク
Kun: きた
Kyūjitai: 业
Componentes: 匕


Etimología
From zh sit-pro *bə(q)  to carry (on back), shoulder. | The sense of north is derived from back (of body): back → to turn the back to; to retreat → north. | The ancient Chinese value the southern direction and houses are traditionally oriented along a north–south axis, as evident in the fengshui theory and in the orientation of buildings in Chinese Neolithic sites. North is the direction the back is oriented to when the person is facing south. | Compare the graphical origin of 南 (Sagart, 1988). | Note the irregular Mandarin reflex (běi) from Middle Chinese (unlike the Cantonese reflex, whose form is regular). Expected is bo (no tone specified because Mandarin reflex tone is unpredictable for Middle Chinese checked syllables), which is nevertheless noted as a literary variant below (namely, bò).

On: ショウ
Kun: たくみ
Kyūjitai: 匞
Componentes: 匚, 斤


Etimología
Several etymologies have been proposed: | * Related to bo བྱང  skilled (Bodman, 1980) or bo སྤྱང  skilful; clever (Sagart and Baxter, 2012). These comparisons would require the och - reconstruction to have a *sb- initial, which is possible if 匚 is considered to be the phonetic component. The Middle Chinese initial would be derived as such: *s.b- > *zb- > *bz- > *dz- (Baxter and Sagart, 2014). | * Schuessler (2007), who reconstructs the och - minimally as *dzaŋh, deems it more likely to be from zh mkh, comparing it to km ចាំង  to dress; to trim (wood) (Schuessler, 2007). | * Jacques (2015) proposes another zh sit etymology, comparing it to bo མཛངས  wise; intelligent, which is derived from bo བཟང  good. Under this hypothesis, it can be derived from 臧 good, which has been connected to the Tibetan word. He postulates the derivation to consist of the nominalizing circumfix *k- -s and the applicative prefix *N-, yielding *k-N-tsaŋ-s > *k-dzaŋ-s.

There were two pronunciations in Middle Chinese. The rising tone pronunciation originally meant “to put away, to eliminate” (causative of “to go away”), and the falling tone “to go away, to leave, to depart” (anticausative). The merger of the two pronunciations already happened in Old Chinese and most extant dialects do not observe this distinction now. | This word is of Sino-Tibetan origin with the basic meaning of “to get rid of”. Compare bo སྐྱག  to spend, to lay out; dung, excrement, bo རྐྱག  dirt, excrement, my ကျ  to fall, to become low, my ချ  to put down, to bring down, to lower.

Maybe same word as 周 to surround as words for “help, aid” often derive from the notion “next to, or around, a person” (for analogies, 佐 to assist < to be on one’s left-side from 左 left and 佑 to assist < to be on one’s right-side from 右  right) (Schuessler, 2007). | :Alternatively, note km ជួយ  to help, assist; to support; to rescue, save (ibid.). Even so, also note th ช่วย, which in turn is from Middle Chinese 助); if km ជួយ and th ช่วย were related, then km ជួយ cannot be related to Old Chinese 周. | ;dynasty’s name | :Attested in the Huayuanzhang East Oracle Bone Inscription HYZ 327.1 (transliterated and translated by Schwartz, 2019) | ::{{zh-x|^周 入 亖{sì}|Zhou contributes four|CL-PC|ref=}} | :A zh 周方白 (Zhōufāng bó, “Elder of Zhou region”), likely King Wen of Zhou, was mentioned in Oracle Bone Inscriptions H11:82 and H11:84 (Lin, 1995) | :Hargett (2021) states that ^商 and ^周 derived from names of “places that the rulers and people of those eras regarded as their homeland or cultic centers”; the 周方 Zhou region was among “areas or regions along the frontier borders of Shang, traditionally regarded as enemy territory”.

;dynasty’s name | :The original semantics are uncertain. Etimología
;“bachelor, man, male” | :*Reminiscent of Austroasiatic synonyms like okz si  male or MK words for “man, male” like *ʔŋsiil, *ensir, *kəsəy on the Malay Peninsula; Schuessler (2007) noted that foreign *-r sometimes left traces in OC initial complex. These relations, if, valid, would keep 士1 “bachelor, man, male” distinct from 士2 “servant, retainer, officer, scholar”. | ;“take or give an office, serve”, “servant”, “retainer”, “officer”, “scholar” | :*Schuessler (2007) noted that one could naturally assume the semantic development “male > man > servant > to serve” in order to posit that 士1 “bachelor, man, male” is the same word as 士2 “servant, retainer, officer, scholar”. Yet, the exopassive derivation 事 “assignment, affair, thing” and Tibeto-Burman counterparts demonstrated no association with “man, maleness”; & “male” hardly derives from “to serve”. | :*Therefore, Schuessler derived these forms from 理 “envoy, jail official, matchmaker” & proposed ultimate zh aav origins. In terms of phonology, MC *dʐ- normally does not occur with *l- and *ʂ in an ST word-family, apparently confirming a non-ST provenance; however, MC *dʐ- here could go back to OC *s-r- (unlike MC *ʂ-, which is from OC *sr) | :*Subsequently, Schuessler posited either relation to Austroasiatic or OC loan into Tibeto-Burman as tbq-pro *ʔ-dzəj  send on an errant (Matisoff, 2003), whence my စာ & bo རྫས  thing, matter, object (Gong, 1999). Even so, Tibeto-Burman cognates of this etymon and 所 are difficult to distinguish.

Related to 汐 evening tide. | Schuessler (2007) suggests it is from zh sit-pro *rV-jak  day; full day; to spend the night; cognate with bo ཞག  day (24 hours), lus riak  to pass the night, kac , my ရက်  day (24 hours), lhu há  night; to pass the night; may also be cognate with 宿 to spend the night and 昔 former times. It is noted that in the oracle bone script, the 24 hour day started and ended some time in the evening or night. Since 日 sun has acquired the meaning of “day (24 hours)”, zh 夕 was then restricted to the time of the day’s end. | On the other hand, STEDT suggests 夕 evening; night was derived from zh sit-pro *ja-n  night, from which 夜 night was also derived. However, zh 夕 was also compared to zh sit-pro *rV-jak  day; full day; to spend the night. Schuessler (2007) assigns Chinese zh 夜 to sit-pro *ja instead, and notes sit-pro *ja and sit-pro *ryak were kept strictly separate in Tibeto-Burman.

However, Baxter and Sagart (2014) may have withdrawn from this theory since they no longer indicate the *t as a prefix. | Also compare tai-pro *ʰlaːjᴬ  many, much, whence th หลาย  many and za lai  many, and qfa-lic-pro *hləːy  many (Gong Qunhu, 2002; Schuessler, 2007; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). kanji/大.title: 大
kanji/大.content:
大

Large, Big


On: ダイ, タイ
Kun: おお-, おお.きい, -おお.いに
Kyūjitai: 亣
Componentes: 一, 人


Etimología
Cognate with 太 too, excessively, 泰 big. Wang (1982) also lists 誕 big, magniloquent, ridiculous as a cognate, which Schuessler (2007) suggests is cognate with 延 to extend instead. There are no unambiguous Tibeto-Burman cognates. Proto-Tibeto-Burman sit-pro *taj  big, from which came Written Tibetan bo མཐེ་བོ  thumb, nun tʰɛ  big, large, great, Mikir tʰè, ketʰè (“big, large, great”), my တယ်  very, is often compared with. There is no final –s in the Tibeto-Burman words, but a –y, which, according to James Matisoff, “indicates emergent quality in stative verbs”. Also compare Chinese 多 many, much, 都 all, as well as my လတ်, which bears particular resemblance to the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction.

kanji/天.title: 天
kanji/天.content:
天

Heavens, Sky, Imperial


On: テン
Kun: あまつ, あめ, あま-
Kyūjitai: 𠀘
Componentes: 一, 大


Etimología
This character was previously reconstructed to have a /*tʰ/-initial in Old Chinese, but this hypothesis has been largely discounted in recent reconstructions, in light of evidence from early Chinese accounts of dialectal pronunciations, transcription of other languages, as well as cognate/derived characters within Chinese, which has all pointed to a voiceless resonant initial /*l̥-/ in Old Chinese. According to [ctext.org/shi-ming/shi-tian/zh chapter 1] of Shiming, by c. 200 , this initial had already produced dialectal variation in the pronunciation: People in central-western China pronounced it with the back of the tongue, like 顯, while people in eastern China pronounced it with the tip of the tongue, like 坦. An old northwestern dialect variant survives as 祆 God of the Zoroastrians, and the word 天竺 India was used to transcribe Old Persian *Hind-uka (“India”). | Further etymology is unknown. During the time when this term was reconstructed with a /*tʰ-/ initial, it was frequently compared with tengri, the name for God in early Turkic and Mongolic peoples’ languages. This now appears unlikely. The only certain external cognate is the bca - (a language closely related to Chinese) word bca heinl  sky, heaven /xẽ⁵⁵/. Chen (1998) proposes cognation with 祁連 and 赫連, transcriptions of a Xiongnu word for “sky”, which he also relates to 昊天.

Therefore, Schuessler (2007) proposes an zh aav origin; compare mkh-pro *d(n)liʔ  large river, sea (whence km ទន្លេ  large river and kdt ). Meanwhile, Schuessler associates similar Hmong languages Hmong forms like cqd tl̥e  river (< hmx-pro *gle) to 溪 “creek, rivulet, rill” instead. | In contrast, Ferlus ([halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/halshs-01182596/file/Ferlus2009_Ethnonyms.pdf 2009]) reconstructs 夷’s Old Chinese pronunciation as [lɨ] and connects 夷 to qfa-tak-pro *k-ri:  Kra-Dai endonym (whence th ไท  “Tai endonym” and lic Hlai  “Hlai endonym”). However, Ferlus concedes that such a derivation of 夷 from *k-ri: “remains speculative, […] not as firmly established as for Hlai and Tai/Thai”.

Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 女, 家


Etimología
Exoactive of 家 home, house, with the addition of the denominal verbalisation suffix *-s in Old Chinese, meaning “to go to one’s new home; to become married”. In the Baxter–Sagart system, an additional pronunciation is posited for the causative sense (“to make someone become married; to marry off”), formed with the prolific Old Chinese causative prefix *s-. Compare *娶.

On: シ, ス, ツ
Kun: こ, -こ, ね

Componentes: 子


Etimología
;child | :zh :inh sit-pro:*tsəʔ | :From zh sit-pro *tsəʔ. | :Cognate with 字, 慈, 滋, 孳 to breed, to propagate. | ;first earthly branch | :In oracle bone and Western Zhou bronze inscriptions, zh 子 had been the sixth earthly branch which later supplanted the original first earthly branch, one of whose written forms – zh 𢀇 – survives in Shuo Wen (Matsumaru, 2015). | :Smith (2011) proposes the first earthly branch had been *甾. Observing that *甾 is closely linked with *緇 dark, stained, *淄 murky (water), 菑 field cleared by burning (all pronounced *tsrə), he proposes that initially the first earthly branch 甾 had meant “darkened, voided, the darkened stage”  and had denoted the new moon phase (ibid.). Meanwhile, 子 had originated from a Sino-Tibetan root meaning “to come forth” and had denoted the moon’s “coming forth” stage (i.e. early waning-gibbous phase) (ibid.). | :Sometime in Warring States period, a change occurred that zh 子 became the first earthly branch and 巳 filled the void of the sixth earthly branch (Matsumaru, 2015), “due to phonological closeness (combined with the semantic opacity of the Branch terms at later eras)” (Smith, 2011). | :Association with the rat was possibly arbitrary, analogous to how 辰, the fifth earthly branch, was arbitrarily associated with the dragon (Ferlus, 2013).

kanji/將.title: 將
kanji/將.content:
將

Commander, General, Admiral

Kun: まさ.に, はた, ひきい.る, もって
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 爿, 𠂊, 冫, 寸


Etimología
A conflation of two roots: “to take; to hold” and “will; be going to; near”. | ; “to take; to hold” (Pronunciations 1, 2 and 3) | : zh sit: compare bo འཆང. | ; “will; be going to; near” (Pronunciation 1) | : zh aav: compare km ចង់ < okz caṅa  to wish, to want. Cognate with 且 about to; on the point of; moreover; also (Wu, 2015). | ; anteposed object introductory particle | : Pulleyblank (1995) notes that 將 as well as several other particles like 唯 and 必 could in Early Classical Chinese topicalize a noun phrase, including predicate objects who are recapitulated with the verb by the pronoun 是, leading effectively to a construction in the form of “將 O 是 V” (“to V O”), which he notes is superficially similar to the later colloquial usage of 將 and 把.

Reasoning that 嵩 and 崧 are the same word and the latter’s phonetic 松 suggests the medial *-l-, Schuessler (2007) minimally reconstructs Old Chinese pronunciation *suŋ < *sluŋ, proposes that it was from zh aav and compares it to mkh-pro *slu(u)ŋ *sluŋ ~ *sluuŋ high. However, note Baxter & Sagart (2014)‘s reconstructions *嵩 ~ 崧, & 松 without medial *-l-. | In any case, note similarities to tai-swe-pro *suːŋᴬ¹, whence th สูง.

On: セン
Kun: かわ
Kyūjitai: 巛
Componentes: 川


Etimología
The Middle and Old Chinese reconstruction of this word is phonologically problematic (STEDT): | * Karlgren (1957) notes that the Middle Chinese form is irregular based on evidence from Shijing rimes. | * Based on velar contacts in the same phonetic series, e.g. *巛, *甽 and *訓, Baxter (1992) and Schuessler (2007) reconstruct the word with a velar initial (Handel, 1998; Sagart, 1999), which undergoes irregular palatalization in the development to Middle Chinese (Baxter, 1992). | * Based on other characters in the same phonetic series, e.g. *順 and *馴, Sagart (1999), and later, Baxter and Sagart (2014), reconstructs zh 川 with a lateral initial and suggests that only a *t- prefix would account for the Middle Chinese initial /t͡ɕʰ/. | Schuessler (2007) relates this word to sit-pro *kl(j)u(ŋ/k)  river; valley, whence 江 river, 谷 valley, bo ཀླུང  river, my ချောင်း  stream. STEDT notes that this does not account for the *-n coda. | STEDT instead compares it to tbq-pro *s-turʔ *m-t(w)əj-n ~ m-ti-s water; fluid; liquid; river; soak; spit, whence 涕 tears, tbq-kuk-pro *tuj  water; fluid; liquid, cdm तीः  water; rain; river; this depends on a reconstruction with a dental initial and requires positing an *‑n suffix not present in Tibeto-Burman languages.

Alternatively, Schuessler thinks this sense’s zh aav origin more likely. Indeed, a late Han (漢) dynasty’s word for “cotton”, 幏布 *ka(H)-puoH (Shuowen Jiezi Shuowen, Book of the Later Han Hou Hanshu), was borrowed from the Austroasiatic-speaking Nanman Man-Dongyi Yi peoples, and a Sanskrit loan (c. 430 CE) into Northwestern dialect is 古貝 *koX-peiH. Compare aav-pro *k-rn-pas and mkh-pro *kpaas  cotton, whence km ក្របាស, bdq kơpaih, mkh-vie-pro *k-paːs (→ vi vải & mtq pái). | :Additionally, Schuessler suggests that the Austroasiatic word was the source of sa कर्पास & grc κάρπασος. kanji/弩.title: 弩
kanji/弩.content:
弩

Bow (arrow)


On: ド
Kun: おおゆみ, いしゆみ
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 奴, 弓


Etimología
Compare tbq-pro  *s-na crossbow, whence duu tana, nxq daqna. | Unger (1990) suggests a derivation from 努 to tense; to exert, as the crossbow shoots arrows by releasing elastic potential energy stored in its limbs. Ferlus (1999) cites Gernet’s opinion that 砮 stone arrow-tip had been semantically extended to mean the whole crossbow. | More likely, 弩 and tbq-pro  *s-na crossbow were Sinitic and Tibeto-Burman renditions of a Mainland Southeast Asia linguistic area Mainland Southeast Asian Wanderwort (Ratliff, 2010), possibly of zh aav origin (Norman and Mei, 1976; Benedict, 1990; Schuessler, 2007). Compare other MSEA lexical items meaning “crossbow”: | * mkh-pro *snaʔ, whence vi ná, km ស្នា; | * hmx-pro *nhaᴮ, whence mww hneev, ium hnaav; | * tai-pro *ʰnwɯəꟲ, whence th หน้าไม้, lo ໜ້າໄມ້, khb ᦐᦱᧉᦺᦙᧉ. | Also compare map-pro *panaq  to shoot (an arrow) (cf. mkh-pro *paɲʔ) whence ms panah, tl pana panà, haw pana. | In contrast, Pain (2020) tentatively proposes a native Chinese origin for 弩, which would then be borrowed in Proto-Vietic language Proto-Vietic and thence into other Austroasiatic languages as well as Tai languages Tai.

kanji/您.title: 您
kanji/您.content:
您

Honorific For “you”


On: ジ, ニ
Kun: なんじ, しかり, その, のみ
Kyūjitai: 恁
Componentes: 你, 心


Etimología
This character was not listed in Sui dynasty Sui/Tang dynasty Tang rhyme books. First attested in Jin dynasty Jin/Yuan dynasty Yuan-era literature, when it was also written as *恁 and probably pronounced as *nim at the time (Lü, 1940; Norman, 1988). The pronoun was used both in the singular and the plural. | The pronoun used in Jin/Yuan-era literature is generally thought to be a fusion of 你們 you (plural) or 你每 you (plural) (Lü, 1940; Norman, 1988). Compare 怹 he, she (polite) ( < 他們 they). | The honorific usage may simply be a development of the plural usage (Norman, 1988); compare en you, fr vous. However, others have argued for a different etymology for the honorific pronoun. Wang (1984) and Lü (1985) argue that it is a contraction of *你老 you (honorific for seniors): /ni lau/ → /nil/ → /nin/. Alternatively, Zhang (2001) suggests that it comes from 仁, an honorific used in Buddhist texts from the Han dynasty. | In yue - and hak -, this character is simply read as *你; in nan-tws -, it is read as *汝.

kanji/愛.title: 愛
kanji/愛.content:
愛

Love, Affection, Favourite


On: アイ
Kun: いと.しい, かな.しい, め.でる, お.しむ, まな
Kyūjitai: 㤅
Componentes: 爫, 冖, 𢖻


Etimología
Based on Baxter’s (1992) och - reconstruction /*ʔɨts/, STEDT suggests that it is from zh sit-pro *ŋ-(w)aːj  to copulate; to love; to be gentle. Compare kar-pro *ʔai  to love, whence blk, ksw အဲၣ်  to love; bfs e⁴⁴  love; lus hmangaih hma-ngaih to love, to like; kac nwai  to respect, to love, kac ngwi  to be gentle; my ငွေ့. The Chinese word is related to a Tibeto-Burman allofam without initial *ŋ-. STEDT states that an och - reconstruction of /*ʔɨjs/ for zh 愛 is also possible because och - rhyming does not provide direct evidence of contacts with -t. | However, Baxter and Sagart (2014) reconstructs /[q]ˁə[p]-s/, which ends in *-p-s instead. The och - contrast between *-p-s and *-t-s was lost at a late stage of och -. The final *-p is not reflected in the tbq comparandum provided by STEDT, making the likelihood that the Chinese form is related to the rest very low (Sagart, 2019). Behr (2016) suggests a derivation from a verbal root meaning “to draw in; to inhale; to suck in”, relating it to 吸, 欱, 愾, 僾, 氣. | 愛 may also be compared with 旡 and 噯 (“to choke; to belch”), as well as 慨 and 嘅 (“sigh; sighing sound; to sigh with emotion”), perhaps through a semantic development “blocked breath; choking” → “held within; stored inside” → “unable to let go; to cherish; to value” → “to love”.

Etimología
From zh sit-pro *ŋa. Cognate with 吾, my ငါ, hak 𠊎. The expected Mandarin pronunciation is ě (now only found in a few Northern dialects); wǒ is “a col[loquial] archaism” (Schuessler, 2007).  | Schuessler further decomposes 我 *ŋâiʔ (his reconstruction) into *ŋa + *i, which he terms an “independent suffix” which also appears in some Tibeto-Burman cognates of this pronoun. DeLancey and Benedict believe that the *-i here was an “information structure marker”. But given how Sagart believes 我 was originally plural (Sagart 1999:142) and DeLancey discovered that first-person plural compounds of sit-pro *ŋa and sit-pro *i exist in e.g. Raji and Stau, it is also possible that the -iʔ element is actually sit-pro *i fused onto the singular.

STEDT compares this word to zh sit-pro *g-(t)sjəw-k/ŋ  wing; hand based on Karlgren’s Archaic Chinese (och -) reconstruction *śi̯ôg, connecting it to bo གཤོག  wing. | However, this comparison is not supported by more recent scholarship, in which the och - is reconstructed with an alveolar nasal (Unger, 1995; Zhengzhang, 1995; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). Evidence for the nasal initial is given in Sagart (1999): | * *杻 handcuffs can be written as *杽, so 丑 (with a nasal initial) and zh 手 seem to be interchangeable as phonetics. | * The ancient graph *丑 resembles the graph of *又 right hand. 狃 animal track; claw seems to be the modern specialized form of *丑, which has been borrowed to represent an earthly branch. | As done by Sagart (1999), Baxter and Sagart (2014) put 杻 handcuffs and 狃 animal track; claw into the same word family as 手. Zhengzhang (1995) suggests a connection to the my  ညှိုး in my လက်ညှိုး  forefinger, which STEDT derives from zh sit-pro *s-njuŋ ~ *s-m-juŋ ~ *s-m-juw  finger. See zh sit-pro *C-njuʔ for more. | Alternatively, Schuessler (2007) suggests a tone B endoactive derivation from 收 to take; to gather, literally “that which is doing the taking”.

On: ダ, ダアス

Componentes: 扌, 丁


Etimología
This post-classical word (its earliest extant attestation is in Shuowen) was pronounced *teŋ in Late Old Chinese, as would be expected from a *丁 phonetic. By the early Ming dynasty Ming period, the character had been borrowed (訓讀) for another word with the same meaning but a different pronunciation, without the nasal ending. This may be related to the previous reading, as a dialectal variant. In Mandarin and some other varieties, the new reading became standard; however, derivations of the older pronunciation are still used in other varieties such as Wu and Min Nan, as well as Vietnamese (vi đánh). | It has been compared to lus dêng  to throw; to fling; to hammer and proposed to be from zh sit (Schuessler, 2007). Also compare mkh-pro *dah *dah ~ daʔ to hit, to meet, whence mnw ဒး  to hit (a mark), meet with, reach [goal], be correct, apposite, to fit and km ទះ  to slap, to strike. | vi đá, despite superficial semantic and phonetic similarities, as well as Nôm attestations of zh 打 being used to write the Vietnamese term, appears to be unrelated. | The pronunciation da is recorded in zh 六書故 as zh 都假切.

Etimología
From zh sit-pro *(p/b)ljaŋ  straight; straighten (STEDT; Schuessler, 2003, 2007). Compare my ဖြောင့်, as well as the following Chinese terms: | * 𡈼 good, virtuous; to be good at | * 庭 straight (of growing grain), upright (of morality); courtyard | * 梃 stick, staff, club | * 筳 bamboo rod | * 鋌 metal rod, ingot | * 珽 jade scepter | The Sino-Tibetan root is allofamic with sit-pro *(p/b)ljaŋ (whence 平 flat, even) and sit-pro *(p/b)liŋ (whence 盈 to fill; full, surplus), with the semantic core of these roots being a “complete realization of a dimensional quality”. | The intensifier usage “quite; very” is most likely a grammaticalized usage from “outstanding; prominent” (Liu, 2008; Yang, 2021). Alternatively, it may be from zh mnc ᡨᡝᠨ  extreme (Aixinjueluo, 1993).

Middle Chinese distinguishes 推 to push and 推 to proceed; to promote; to deduce. | Older Mandarin dictionariesSamuel Wells Williams, 1874; Herbert Allen Giles, 1892 give chuī (the Mandarin reflex of 推 ) as a variant reading for all senses, while Cantonese dictionariesJohn Chalmers, 1855; Samuel Wells Williams, 1856; 廣話國語一貫未定稿, 1916 only assign ceoi1 to the “to deduce” sense (e.g. in *推測 - to surmise). Most modern Sinitic varieties use the reflexes of 推  for all meanings, while Sino-Xenic use the reflexes of 推  (in Korean, however, the reflex of 推  is also used in a few words). Some varieties (including certain Hakka, Min, and sometimes Yue dialects) preserve both readings, but not necessarily disambiguate them by meaning. | Outside of Sinitic, Schuessler (2007) adduces cdm दुस् as a cognate. Note also similarities to my တိုး. | See also 揣. | ; “to support”; “oshi” | : zh ja - 推し おし.

擔

Carry, Bear, Undertake


On: タン
Kun: かつ.ぐ, にな.う
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 扌, 詹


Etimología
According to STEDT, from zh sit-pro *tam  to carry on shoulder, whence my ထမ်း  to carry on the shoulder. Schuessler (2007), on the other hand, notes 擔 is an area word whose source is probably Austroasiatic; compare mkh-pro *klam ~ *kləm  to carry on shoulder, whence kjg. An alternative form with initial *t which agrees with later Old Chinese is widespread; compare also km ទាំ  to tire of; to bear, km ទ្រាំ  to bear; to endure, hmx-pro *ntam  to carry on shoulder, whence ium daːm¹, and tai-pro *trwaːmᴬ  to carry on the back, whence th หาม  to carry. | The softened initial in Northern Min points to OC pre-nasalization which is supported by ium daːm¹ (Schuessler, 2007), an early Chinese loan into Hmong-Mien (Baxter and Sagart, 2014). | 擔 is 擔 with the passive s/h-suffix, literally “what is carried”.

; “side; square; region” | : Probably related to 旁, 傍 (Schuessler, 2007). | ; “parallel boats” | : Cognate with 舫, 艕. According to STEDT, from zh sit-pro *poŋ  raft; float; compare my ဖောင်  raft, kac hpong  kac. According to Schuessler (2007), this etymon is an area word; compare th พ่วง  raft; pontoon, map-pro *qabaŋ  boat, omx  kɓaŋ ship; boat. | ; “just now”; “now” | : Cognate with 甫. Compare kac hpang  to begin, tbq-kuk-pro *pran  to begin (STEDT). | ; “method; law” | : Etymology not certain. May be the same word as 方. Cognate with 仿. Perhaps cognate with bo བྱང་བ  skill; experience, bo སྦྱངས  trained; exercised studied (Schuessler, 2007). Alternatively, it may belong to km ព្រាង  to draft; to sketch < km រាង  shape; form; figure. If so, it belongs to an Austroasiatic allofam which includes 狀. “Law; norm; standard” is a common extension of “form; shape”.

kanji/是.title: 是
kanji/是.content:
是

Just So, This, Right, Justice


On: ゼ, シ
Kun: これ, この, ここ
Kyūjitai: 昰
Componentes: 日, 𤴓


Etimología
“This [an independent pronoun] > this, it [object recapitulation], be right, correct, so > to be, indeed”. The modern copulative sense only emerged by the Eastern Han dynasty (Dobson, 1964; Norman, 1988; Zürcher, 2013), and gradually replaced the archaic 唯 to be and the classical copulative construction with 也.  | This was due to the lack of a left-branching copula as archaic 唯 shifted into a contrasting and restricting particle, as well as its frequent use in presentational copulative constructions, often in the form of “A, 是 B 也” (“A, this is B”), which led to it being gradually reinterpreted as the copula instead of 也. Also note the semantic opposition with literary negative copula 非 as in “right” and “wrong”, which emerged by the Warring States period from the frequent collocation of the expression “是 X 也, 非 Y 也” (This is X, not Y) (Pulleyblank, 1995) .  | To understand this development, compare 之 him, it, this > possessive, 其 he, his, its > dialectal possessive. Compare French fr c’est which in colloquial speech often replaces copula fr est. | From zh sit-pro *m-daj ~ m-di  that; this. In Chinese, cognate with 寔 this (subject contrastive) , 實 this (subject contrastive) , 之 this; him; her; it (oblique) , 諟 to examine, to consider. In Tibeto-Burman, cognate with bo དེ  that, kac dai, kac ndai  this, and my ဒီ  this.

Cognate with bo འགུགས  to bend, my ကောက်  bent, curved, crooked (Hill, 2019). Compare mkh-pro *gɔk  be crooked, bent, lame (Schuessler, 2007). | ; song | : Of zh origin. Shuowen claims that it derives from the “turn” sense as describing a melodic contour (compare, for example, English’s use of en turn to describe a musical figure), but most modern scholars doubt this connection, mostly interpreting the depicted bent object as a wind instrument instead. However, a number of other suggestions have been put forth—a rice container, a basket, a tract of farmland, and so on—which, if correct, would invalidate any obvious direct link between shape and sense. kanji/月.title: 月
kanji/月.content:
月

Month, Moon


On: ゲツ, ガツ
Kun: つき
Kyūjitai: 𡇹
Componentes: 月


Etimología
From zh sit-pro *s-ŋʷ(j)a-t  moon; star, whence also Magar language Magar und , tbq-lob-pro *mwatᴸ (whence lhu məʔkə məʔ-kə), duu gurmet  star (Matisoff, 1980; LaPolla, 1987; STEDT). | Various alternative etymologies have also been proposed: | * Unger (1992) proposes cognation with bo ངོ  waxing and waning moon; half moon (as in bo མར་ངོ  waning moon and bo ཡར་ངོ  waxing moon), which Schuessler (2007) connects to sit-pro *s-ŋow  white; light colour. However, Sagart (1999) points out that the Tibetan word may be analyzed as a derivative of bo ངོ  face, which would mean the semantic connection between “moon” and “face” had to occur either independently in Chinese and Tibetan or in Proto-Sino-Tibetan; it also requires positing a suffix und -t in Chinese. | * Pulleybank (1995a) proposes another etymology based on the glyph for zh 名 (reconstructed as und *màŋʲ), which he analyses as a phono-semantic compound of phonetic zh 夕 and semantic zh 口. He suggests that the phonetic component represents a lost word und *màŋʲ  moon, and reconstructs zh 月 as und *mŋʲ (consonantal frame of “moon”) + und *-at (suffix) > und *ŋʲʷat. However, there are more straightforward ways of explaining the glyph origin of zh 名 (see there), which would nullify the hypothesis of the lost word. | * Related to zh 越 in some way. | ** Mei (1979) derives zh 月 from 越: und **N-gjot > *ngwjat. Also in this proposed word family is 歲 year. The semantics of this word family is centred around “to pass; to elapse”. While Matisoff (1980) seems supportive of this word family, STEDT reconstructs tbq-pro *ɢʷrat *grwat to travel; to go through for zh 越 and zh 歲, separate from the root for zh 月. | ** Ferlus (2012) reconstructs the och - as und *ŋ.wat and puts it in a word family formed from a Chinese root und *wat, having a meaning of “circularity” or “circular boundary”. This proposed word family includes 越, as in “to cross the enclosure of the village”, and 外, as in “out of the enclosure of the village”.

え | ja: | Celtis sinensis | thumb|250px|ja 榎: the Chinese hackberry tree. | From ja ojp -. Found as an independent noun in the Man’yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE. | Some references suggest various theories regarding the ultimate derivation of this e.  However, historical kana usage indicates different roots. | * From ja 枝  branch, from the many branches. | * From ja 柄  handle, from the way the wood was used for tool handles. | ** ja 柄 derives from ja 枝, and both originate from an older pronunciation of /je/ (ye), phonologically distinct from ja 榎, which was just /e/ (e) in the oldest sources. For example, ja 榎 and ja 枝 were used in the Ametsuchi no Uta, a pangram similar to the Iroha, written prior to the merger of /e/ and /je/. | * From ja 餌  food for animals, from the multitude of berries eaten by birds. | ** This originates from an older pronunciation of /we/ (we), again phonologically distinct from ja 榎. | Consequently, this ja 榎 appears to be a distinct and separate root, independent of these other terms.

Componentes: 一, 止


Etimología
Sino-Tibetan or area word: “centre; target; first (month); straight; correct”. | Compare lus dîng  to go straight or direct (as person, arrow etc.); to go straight through without breaking the journey; straight; direct. Matisoff sets up zh sit-pro *m-tjak/ŋ ~ tik/ŋ  good; very; real; straight for this, which includes zh 正, 直 straight; right and 實 solid; true. | Additionally, Matisoff has zh sit-pro *t(r)waŋ  straight; straighten, whence cdm धेङ्‌सा  straight, kac ding  straight, bo དྲང་པོ  straight; correct; upright; just; fair, my တန်း  straight; to head straight for. Also compare km ទៀង  accurate; correct; exact; precise; honest and th ดิ่ง. | Derivatives: | * 征 to go straight > to go on a journey | * 政 correct; to govern; government; to determine | * 整 orderly; to arrange; to dispose | For etymology of pronunciation 正 in the month 正月’s name, see there.

kanji/歲.title: 歲
kanji/歲.content:
歲

year


On: サイ, セイ
Kun: とし, よわい
Kyūjitai: 嵗
Componentes: 步, 戉


Etimología
A derivative of 越 to pass over (Mei, 1979, 1992). Ultimately probably from zh sit-pro *ɢʷrat  to travel; to go through; compare bo སྐྱོད  to go (Mei, 1979, 1992; Gong Hwang-cherng, 2002; STEDT). | The functions of the *s- prefix and the *-s suffix are not clear. Possible explanations include: | * *s- as a directive prefix and *-s as a nominalizer (Mei, 1992); | * *s- is an iterative prefix, literally “to pass on again” (Schuessler, 2007); | * *s- (possibly with *-s) as a nominalizer (Smith, 2012). | Alternatively, it may be derived from a word like 圓 round; circle (< zh sit-pro *wal  round; circular), literally “to start the circle/cycle again” (Schuessler, 2007). | Outside of Sino-Tibetan, this word has been compared to th ขวบ  year, which Bodman (1980) considers to be a loan from Chinese, as well as map-pro *kawaS  year; season; sky (Sagart, 2005). | Also see Schuessler (2007) and Smith (2012) for a discussion on the semantic development of this word, especially the connection between “Jupiter” and “year”.

kanji/水.title: 水
kanji/水.content:
水

Water


On: スイ
Kun: みず, みず-
Kyūjitai: 𡿭
Componentes: ㇇, 亅, 乀, 丿


Etimología
zh:,yue:,lzh:,gan:,hak:súi,cdo:cūi,nan:chúi,wuu: | Here are some proposals:  | * zh sit-pro *lwi(j)  flow; stream (Benedict, 1974; Coblin, 1986; Handel, 1998; Schuessler, 2007; STEDT). Cognate with lus lui  stream; brook; river, ctd   stream; river, kac lawi  to flow (as water). | **och 水, as reconstructed by Schuessler, is sit root’s endoactive derivation with suffix *-ʔ, meaning “that which is flowing”; its voiceless initial suggests the presence of a nominalizing prefix *k- or *s-. Another derivative from the sit root is possibly och 泫 (minimally reconstructed). | **Compare also areal etyma aav-pro *loːjʔ  to wade; to swim and tai-pro *loːjᴬ  to swim. | *Gong (1995) reconstructs och - *hljədx and compares it to bo ཆུ  water, which STEDT derives from tbq-pro *tsju  water; liquid; bodily fluid. | *Baxter and Sagart (2014), employing evidence from the Proto-Min form of the Min colloquial variant zh 沝, reconstructs the latter *turʔ and thereby reconstructs och - *s.turʔ, and compares it to tbq-pro *twəj  to flow; to suppurate, which is likely related to what STEDT notates as tbq-pro *s-turʔ *m-t(w)əy-n ~ m-ti-s (STEDT). *s.turʔ was then followed by an Eastern dialectal variant, *s.tujʔ, which leads to Early Middle Chinese *sywijX. | *Like Gong (1995), Sagart (2017) compares *水 to bo ཆུ, but he also compares it to brx दै, lus tui, kar-pro *thejᴬ, for which he tentatively  derives from zh sit-pro *s-turʔ. | ** Meanwhile STEDT derives said non-Sinitic items from tbq-pro *s-turʔ *m-t(w)əy-n ~ m-ti-s.  | * Handel thinks *水 is unlikely to be related to tbq-pro *tsju and tbq-pro *m-t(w)əj-n ~ m-ti-s because of phonological issues (STEDT).

kanji/河.title: 河
kanji/河.content:
河

River


On: カ
Kun: かわ
Kyūjitai: 𢀎
Componentes: 氵, 可


Etimología
Originally particularly used for the Yellow River, with other rivers known as 水. Later extended generally as a word for rivers in northern China but the influence of 江 Yangtze River; river in southern China has meant that modern usage tends to favor it for shorter rivers and creeks except in historical cases. | Further etymology uncertain. Various hypotheses have been proposed: | * zh sit. Either: | ** Cognate with bo རྒལ  to cross, to traverse (Coblin, 1986), or  | ** Derived from 湖 lake (Matisoff, 1995), or | ** that the Yellow River’s name stems from the shape, which resembles an adze handle 柯, of a stretch spanning 500 to 600 kilometers “from Hejin Héjīn, Tong Pass Tóngguān to east of Zhengzhou Zhèngzhōu” (Takashima, 2012). | * A Mongolic loan. Compare xgn-pro *gowl  river > mn ᠭᠣᠣᠯ  river (Norman and Mei, 1976). This was argued against in Zhang (1998).  | ** Miyake (2017) surmises that xgn-pro *gowl  river and 河, even if related, might have come from a third source language, e.g. Xiongnu language Xiongnu. If so, compare also qfa-yen-pro *xur₁  water in light of Xiongnu’s speculated linguistic affinity with the Yeniseian languages.

On: ルイ, レイ
Kun: なみだ
Kyūjitai: 淚
Componentes: 氵, 戻


Etimología
なみだ | From ja ojp -. Ultimately from ja jpx-pro *namita. | Attested in the Nihon Shoki with the man’yōgana spelling 那%瀰%多 な%み%た. The Kojiki and Man’yōshū have 那%美%多 な%み%た, and the Man’yōshū also has later instances where the 多 た was replaced with 太 だ, forming 奈%美%太 な%み%だ, indicating a phonetic change over time from namita to namida. | Ultimate derivation ja. There are interesting phonetic and semantic similarities with th น้ำตา  tear, overlapping semantically with ko 눈물  tear, perhaps pointing to an ancient prehistoric borrowing. Alexander Vovin lists it among “naturalized loanwords from Korean”. However, such similarities may also be purely accidental.

kanji/深.title: 深
kanji/深.content:
深

On: シン
Kun: ふか.い, -ぶか.い, ふか.まる, ふか.める, み-
Kyūjitai: 㴱
Componentes: 氵, 罙


Etimología
Unger (1995) suggests that 深 had Old Chinese initial *n- because of 淰’s phonetic component 念. | Schuessler (2007) reconstructs 深 & proposes relations to lus hniam  to be low, to sink into (land), my နိမ့်သေ နိမ့် low, nmf, bo ནེམས་  sink a little, give way, which Schuessler traces to tbq-pro *nem  low, which STEDT in turn derives from sit-pro *s-n(i/u)(ː)p/m ~ *r/s-nyap/m  pinch, squeeze; press, oppress; submerge, sink into, west, low, soft. If so, 深 is from zh sit-pro -. | Schuessler also notices 深’s similarity to 沉, which he considers to be an Mainland Southeast Asia linguistic area areal etymon. | Possibly cognate with 探 and 揇 (however, see there). | 深, “depth” (in Rites of Zhou) & whence MC ɕiɪmH, is nominal derivation with suffix *-s (> departing tone). | 淰, “be startled and flee (of fish); i.e. to sink into the deep” (in Liji) & whence Mandarin shěn, is endoactive derivative with *-ʔ (> rising tone).

Destroy, Ruin, Overthrow, Perish


On: メツ
Kun: ほろ.びる, ほろ.ぶ, ほろ.ぼす
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 氵, 烕


Etimología
From zh sit-pro *s-miːt  to extinguish; to shut abruptly; to wink; to blink; to die. Matisoff compares my မှိတ်  (of eyes) to close; (of light) to put out, to switch off and possibly bo མེད  to not exist. Cognate Chinese characters include: | * 烕 to destroy; to cause destruction | * 蔑 to destroy | The Old Chinese *e ~ Proto-Tibeto-Burman *i vowel discrepancy may be explained by a reanalysis of the proto-etymon in Chinese, as derived from 隳 to destroy + suffix *-t (Schuessler, 2009), although *隳 is reconstructed in the Baxter-Sagart and Zhengzhang systems as having an *l-like initial. The direct Chinese comparandum of Proto-Tibeto-Burman *mit may be 沒 to disappear; to die; to perish in water (ibid.).

zh :inh sit-pro:*məj | Possibly from zh sit-pro *məj (Schuessler 2007; STEDT). However, see there for phonological problems. | Sagart and Baxter (2024) update their Old Chinese reconstruction to 火 *X.pˤərʔ}} (whence Middle Chinese MC xwaX → huǒ) and propose alternative cognacy to 燹 *X.pər(ʔ)-s}} (whence MC xwijH), both being prefixed by unknown element X- which turned the labial plosive *p(ʰ)- into the fricative *xw-; moreover, both are cognates to 燹 *sə-pˤər(ʔ)-s}} (whence MC senX → xiǎn). They also propose that aforesaid Chinese words are cognates to tbq-pro *par (i.e. STEDT Etymon #2152 tbq-pro *bʷar ~ *pʷar  fire; burn; kindle; roast, see [stedt.berkeley.edu/~stedt-cgi/rootcanal.pl/etymon/2152 there] for descendants) as well as map-pro *dapuʀ  cooking fire, hearth.

kanji/為.title: 為
kanji/為.content:
為

Do, Change, Make, Benefit, Welfare, Be Of Use, Reach To, Try, Practice, Cost, Serve As, Good, Advantage, As A Result Of


On: イ
Kun: ため, な.る, な.す, す.る, たり, つく.る, なり
Kyūjitai: 爲
Componentes: 為


Etimología
The two pronunciations below (“to make; to do; to be”, “for; to; because”) are cognate; the latter is the *–s derivative of the former. Words meaning “to make, to do” often have secondary meanings of “for, as” – compare *作. | Etymology not certain. Starostin compared this word with bo བགྱིད  to make, to manufacture, bo བགྱི་བ  action, deed, bo ཡིན  is, be and my ဝေ  to distribute, to share. Schuessler (2007) listed mkh-pro *ʔaajh  to give (> km ឲ្យ  to give, to donate) and km ធ្វើ  to do, to make, although the vowels do not match. | The graphic representation using a monkey or an elephant probably stems from a homophonic or near-homophonic etymon which was rarely attested; compare sit-pro *b/g-woj-n > kac woi  monkey and possibly 猿 ape. STEDT considers this word to be a possible descendant of zh sit-pro *m-gwi(j)  elephant. Outside Sino-Tibetan, compare mkh-vie-pro *-vɔːj  elephant > vi voi  elephant.

zh:,cdo:Mò̤ | Core Sino–Tibetan. From zh sit-pro *ma  no, not; cognate with bo མ་  not and my မ  not. | Cognate with: | * 微 not, no | * 毋 do not | * 勿 not, don’t | * 未 not yet, haven’t | * 靡 not, no | * 亡 not have; to flee, to disappear, to die | * 沒 to end, to disappear, to drown | * 莫 none, nobody, nothing; do not; can not | Attested profusely in Classical Chinese, this word is the prototypical negation particle in the *m- series of Chinese negatives. In the oracle bone script, however, zh 無 is not frequently used, and its homophone (or near-homophone) 毋 is used instead. | See 不 not for more on negative particles in Old Chinese. | Perhaps related to 巫 shaman, wizard, magician, sorcerer, witch.

Other items in the same word-family are: | * 眩 troubled sight, deluded, deceive, | * 炫 bright, dazzle, show off, | * 瑩 bright, color of jade > kind of gem | * 熲 light, flame, blaze, which is 熒 with *k- nominalizer. | * 榮 flower > flowering, prosperity > glory, which is the same word as 熒. | This word-family could be zh sit-pro - and related to lus ven & lus veng  to be open; to be unobstructed by trees, clouds, etc; to be clear; to be free of clouds; to be bright (as weather) (ibid.).

かた | From ja ojp -, from ja jpx-pro *kata-. First cited in the Nihon Shoki of 720. | Japanese sources describe this as cognate with 方 かた side, direction. However, the pitch accents differ: compounds starting with ja 片 show  accent in the Heian period, in contrast to ja 方, which is recorded with a  accent instead, suggesting no direct relationship between the two.  | Alternatively, 肩 かた might be a more likely cognate given that term’s matching  accent and compounds also indicating homonymy: compare 傾げる かたげる, 担げる かたげる. From some language ancestral to modern hmx languages, from zh hmx-pro *qluwˣ  dog, perhaps from zh map-pro *(u-)(ŋ)kuɣkuɣ  dog (Norman, 1988; Benedict, 1996). | Alternatively, STEDT derives this from zh sit-pro *d-kʷəj-n  dog, whence also 犬. | Less likely, it may be related to 駒 foal, 羔 lamb and 𤘽 calf (Wang, 1982). Excavated Warring States and Qin texts attest 狗子 puppy and 虎狗; the latter is distinguished from an adult zh 虎 by a lower reward in the Yuelu Qin manuscripts. This suggests that zh 狗, like its variant zh 豿, could also denote a young animal or cub.

Here some proposals: | * Fangyan (book) Fangyan [ctext.org/dictionary.pl] and Guo Pu consider it to be one among many dialectal words for 貔, which however is a different word (Schuessler, 2007) (see there). | * Zhao & Huang (1998) (apud Schuessler, 2007) connects it to hmn - pli ~ ple “cat”. | * Schuessler (2007) minimally reconstructs 貍 from *pʰrə ~ *pʰə-rə and proposes possible zh sit etymology and compares it to mro pri  a kind of leopard (see also Löffler, 1966); he also sees potential cognacy with bo ཞི་མི, bo ཞིམ་བུ, bo ཞུམ་བུ - all meaning “cat” - if those were from *ryi-mi; additionally, bo པི་ཤི  cat (< *zhi?) is possibly equivalent to Old Chinese dialectal forms with initial *pʰ- (e.g. 𧳏 < Eastern Han Chinese LHC *pʰiə < OC *pʰrə or 𧳏貍); in that case, the original Chinese word might have been a compound: 貔狸 “(large) cat and small cat”; even so, see 貔 for possible Indic influence on Tibetan byi ~ pi (ibid.). | * STEDT reconstructs zh sit-pro *s-(l/r)e(y/ŋ)  squirrel, weasel and proposes cognacy with 鼪, bo སྲེ་མོང  weasel, my ရှဉ့်  squirrel, etc.

Cognate with mvi にか Tarama, Okinawa Tarama and Minna Island (Tarama, Okinawa) Minna dialects|t=cat}} via unknown Japonic substratum. | Listed in modern references as a compound of ね  にゃ, en mew, meow|こ||pos2=diminutive noun-forming suffix}}. According to the {{w 和名類聚抄 和%名%類%聚%抄|^わ%みょう% ^るい%じゅ%しょう|rom=Wamyō Ruijushō}} of 931–938, neko is a shortening of 猫 ねこま, but neko appears in texts earlier than nekoma: neko is first attested in the Shin’yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794, while nekoma is not attested until 918 in the {{w 本草和名 本%草%和%名|^ほん%ぞう% ^わ%みょう|pos=the oldest surviving dictionary of medicine in Japan}}. | A comparison of accent patterns between the dialects shows some confusion (see dialectal data): | * One group of dialects behaves as if  was the Heian Kyoto accent pattern: many dialects with the Tokyo type accent, including the standard Japanese in Tokyo, pronounce this word with an  pitch pattern, and in some non-mainstream Keihan type dialects as well, this word has a corresponding  pitch pattern. | * Another group of dialects behaves as if  was the Heian Kyoto accent pattern: the mainstream Keihan type dialects pronounce this word with an  pitch pattern, and in a few of the Tokyo type dialects, this word has a corresponding  pitch pattern. | As a result, this term is one example of words that have the same pitch accent pattern between Tokyo and Osaka/Kyoto. The confusion seems to be due to an impression that the term comes from a compound word origin.

kanji/獅.title: 獅
kanji/獅.content:
獅

Lion


On: シ
Kun: しし
Kyūjitai: 師
Componentes: 犭, 師


Etimología
Originally written as *師. The earliest written attestation is a wooden slip (zh Ⅱ90DXT0214S: 55) from the Xuanquan (zh 懸泉置) archive c. 48–13 BCE, recording a lion (*師子) presented to the Han court by an envoy of the king of 折垣. Later attestations in the Eastern Han era include the Book of Han before 111, the surviving portion of the 東觀漢記 Dongguan Hanji {{circa2 150}}, and Lokaksema (Buddhist monk) Lokakṣema’s translation of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā 179. The term is possibly of zh ira origin. In the Book of Han, the lion was described as indigenous to the historical 烏弋山離 Alexandria, a state of the Sistan/Arachosia region identified variously with Alexandria Prophthasia, Alexandria in Arachosia, or the Indo-Parthian Kingdom. The Dongguan mentions a lion as a gift from the Shule Kingdom in the year 133, where a Saka language was spoken then. Earlier definite dates associated with the lion mentioned in the Book of the Later Han include the year 87, when a gift lion from the Yuezhi was recorded. | Compare ira-pro *cárguš. Possibly related to 狻猊. | Meanwhile, possible zh ine-toc connections have been postulated; cf. txb ṣecake and etymologies.

However, reconstructing the och - as *waŋ, he notes the mismatch between Old Chinese *w- vs. Tibetan *b- (unless *dw- can become db-; for possible *b- ~ * w- variation, see *花). He also compares it to Konyak languages Proto-Northern Naga und *waŋ  chief. | * Schuessler (2007) alternatively proposes a connection to okz vāṅ, okz vaṅ km វាំង, “royal palace”}}, which he considers to be cognate with km ហ្លួង  king. This is perhaps supported by a Chinese bronze inscriptions bronze inscription where zh 王 refers to a place, not the Zhou dynasty Zhou king (Shaughnessy, 1991). The semantic shift from “palace” to “king” parallels egy pr-ꜥꜣ  pharaoh, from egy pr  house + egy ꜥꜣ  great, big. The connection to the okz - word would thus relate it to mkh-pro *waŋ *waŋ ~ *waaŋ enclosure; to go round, which is part of a larger aav word family, including 營  to encamp; to surround and 環  ring. Bodman (1980) connects zh 王 with 皇 sovereign, which Schuessler (2007) connects to this word family. | * Speculations exist about its connection to 尪 lame, crippled and 狂 mad, based on theories about the connection between ancient Chinese kingship and shamanism (Keightley, 1995).

Before Qing dynasty, the character was used in word 碼瑙 (Yupian) and 碼頭 (Stories to Awaken the World), both originally written with 馬. | ; “gambling chip”, “chip for counting” (> “number”), “classifier for things” | : Appears in Qing dynasty, also originally written with 馬. See 馬 for more. | ; “yard” | : Used in zh 《英吉利国舆情记略》 (1834), probably a derivation of “counting chip” sense which is used for translating English yard. | ; “kilometer per hour” | : Probably a corruption of 邁 (mile > mile per hour > kilometer per hour). | ; “pixelization” | : 馬賽克. | ; “to reply to a post for reading it later” | : From zh en mark.

On: ウ

Etimología
;insect | :Compare tbq-pro *was  honey, bee (Benedict, 1972) or semantically closer Waic languages Proto-Waic *wak “insect” (Schuessler, 2007), the latter from mkh-pal-pro *ʋaːk  insect, worm (Sidwell, 2015). | ;Yu the Great | :The character is attested in bronze inscriptions from the late Shang dynasty (zh 𫤵禹祖辛罍, zh 𫤵禹祖辛卣). | :The earliest known reference to the legendary Yu in excavated texts is found in the zh 豳公盨 inscription from the mid-Western Zhou: | :{{zh-x|天 命 ^禹 敷 土，墮 山 濬{jùn} 川；乃 仇 方 設 正{zhèng}，降 民 監 德；|Heaven commanded Yu to spread out the land: he broke down the mountains and dredged the rivers, and thereupon established leaders for the various domains. [Heaven] sent down the people and kept watch over their virtue;|CL-PC|ref=Mid-Western Zhou (later phase), zh 豳公盨 inscription|collapsed=y}} | :In the zh 禹盤 (mid-Western Zhou), *禹 appears as the name of a contemporaneous individual: | :{{zh-x|^禹 拜 稽首，對 揚 王 休。^禹 作 文考 ^父-^癸 寶 䵼{pán} 彝，其 永 寶。|Yu bowed and prostrated, in response extolling the king’s beneficence. Yu made this precious pan vessel for his late father Gui; may it be treasured forever.|CL-PC|ref=Mid-Western Zhou, zh 禹盤 inscription|collapsed=y}} | :In the late Western Zhou, the well-known zh 禹鼎 inscription (King Yi of Zhou King Yi period) records the deeds of a military official named 禹 who led an expedition against the Marquis of È (zh 鄂侯馭方): | :{{zh-x|^禹 曰：「丕 顯 桓桓 皇祖 ^穆-公 克 夾 詔 先王 奠 四方，肆 ^武-公 亦 弗 遐 忘 朕 聖 祖考 ^幽-大叔、^懿-叔，命 ^禹 纘{zuǎn} 朕 祖考，政{zhèng} 于 ^井 邦。肆 ^禹 亦 弗 敢 憃{chōng}，惕 共{gōng} 朕 辟 之 命。」|Yu said: “My greatly illustrious and martial august ancestor, Duke Mu, was able to assist the former kings in settling the four quarters. Thus Duke Wu also did not dare forget my sagely forefathers, the Great Uncle You and Uncle Yi, and commanded Yu to carry on [the work of] my ancestors, governing the state of Jing. Thus Yu did not dare act willfully, but reverently upheld the commands of my lord.”|CL-PC|ref=Late Western Zhou (King Yi of Zhou King Yi period), zh 禹鼎 inscription|collapsed=y}} | :The zh 叔向父禹簋 (King Li of Zhou King Li period) records an individual of the same lineage (also referencing the ancestor zh 幽大叔).

Schuessler (2007) also compares it to hmx: mww tub  son, ium dorn  son. | ; “shaman” | : Norman and Mei (1976) proposed that the Min Chinese word for “shaman” (*-dəŋA), written as zh 童, is from an Austroasiatic substratum, cognate with vi đồng, mnw ဒံၚ်  to dance while under daemonic possession; to proceed by leaps, mnw ဒေါၚ်  shaman called in to organise kəlok dances. This is rebutted in Sagart (2008), who cited the wide distribution of the sense “magician; sorcerer” in late 19th-century & early 20th-century Chinese and the secondary meaning of zh 童 as “servant; messenger”, describing the resemblance between the Min and Austroasiatic terms as “undoubtedly fortuitous”.

Attested somewhat late, in Warring States period’s texts. | A Southeast Asian area word ([core.ac.uk/download/pdf/156628995.pdf Alves 2015]). | * Per Schuessler 2007, most likely of zh aav origin. Compare mkh-pro *truŋ  stable, sty, cage and mkh-pro *kruŋ  to confine in [sealang.net/monkhmer/dictionary/ Shorto 2006], whence km ទ្រុង  cage, km ក្រុង  to confine, kdt, potentially vi chuồng  cage; shed; coop, and so forth. The Vietnamese may possibly be an early Chinese loan instead (Alves 2018). | * STEDT reconstructs zh sit-pro *kruːŋ  cage, based on e.g. grt gring  cage, my ချိုင့်. Schuessler thinks these were also borrowed from Austroasiatic. | * Other forms include tai-pro, whence th กรง  cage; and poz-pro *kuruŋ, whence id kurung  cage, tl kulong  caged. Schuessler believes these are also ultimately from Austroasiatic.

kanji/聞.title: 聞
kanji/聞.content:
聞

Hear, Ask, Listen


On: ブン, モン
Kun: き.く, き.こえる
Kyūjitai: 𦔵
Componentes: 門, 耳


Etimología
Schuessler derives this from zh sit-pro *mnam *mnəm to smell, whence bo མནམ་པ  to smell of, bo སྣོམ་པ  to smell, kac manam, my နမ်  to smell, my နံ  to stink (Schuessler, 2007). It is very phonetically difficult, requiring an inversion of n and m in Chinese (which Schuessler attributes to labial dissimilation or prefix-preemption) in addition to rejecting the Baxter-Sagart reconstruction with a *u in favour of reconstructing *ə instead (*u and *ə are difficult to distinguish before *-n). The reconstruction with *u is solidified by rhyming patterns in the Classic of Poetry, making Schuessler’s etymology impossible. | In almost all major Tibeto-Burman languages, this etymon means only “to smell”. Schuessler explains the application of “to hear” in Chinese via various influences. He sees a parallel in Tibeto-Burman *na “ear ~ nose” and hence perhaps in Sino-Tibetan (see sit-pro *r/g-na  ear). The Chinese stem may have converged with a Mon-Khmer etymon (cf. mkh-mnc-pro *smaaɲ  to inquire (ibid.). Schuessler also notes bo མཉན་པ  to listen to; to hear, which he deems phonologically quite close to Chinese. | Pronunciation 2 (“be heard about; renowned; fame”) is a derivation of pronunciation 1, with passive suffix *-s (ibid.). | 問 to ask is the exoactive derivation of pronunciation 1 with suffix *-s, literally “let (me) hear” (ibid.).

On: ト
Kun: はら
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 月, 土


Etimología
A post-classical word. Compare zh sit-pro *l-tjwa  mouth; beak; food; stomach, whence bo ལྟོ་བ  stomach; belly (STEDT). Compare also tai-pro *dwuːŋꟲ  belly (whence th ท้อง) and qfa-kms-pro *luŋ²  stomach, as Middle Chinese shangsheng corresponds to foreign -ŋ in some words (Schuessler, 2007). | Some dialects have different pronunciations for the two senses, “abdomen; belly (of a human)” and “stomach (of an animal)”, derived from two different readings in Middle Chinese that differed in the voicing of the initial consonant. | * In Mandarin, the pronunciation for the former sense derives from the zh 徒古切 reading in Middle Chinese (i.e. the reading with voiced initial /d/) and the pronunciation for the latter sense derives from the zh 當古切 (i.e. the reading with voiceless initial /t/) reading. | * In Min Nan, the pronunciation for the former sense derives from the zh 當古切 reading and the pronunciation for latter sense derives from the zh 徒古切 reading. | * Cantonese uses the same pronunciation for both senses, derived from the zh 徒古切 reading. | * Hakka also uses the same pronunciation for both senses, but it is instead derived from the zh 當古切 reading.

kanji/胳.title: 胳
kanji/胳.content:
胳

Armpit, Arms


On: カク, ギャク
Kun: わき
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 月, 各


Etimología
Possibly from zh sit-pro *tV-lak *lak ~ *C-jak arm; hand; wing. Sagart (1999) considers it to be a prefixed form of a root *lak, found unprefixed as 亦 armpit and with a loosely attached prefix as *ᵃkə-lak, preserved in some southern varieties, such as yue - 胳肋底 gaak3 laak6-1 dai2, cdo - 胳腋下 gó̤k-lŏ̤k-â. In the new reconstruction by Baxter and Sagart (2014), the connection to 亦 is still implied (cf. Sagart, 2007), but the comparison to the forms in the southern varieties no longer holds (Hill, 2019). Zhang, Jacques and Lai (2019) compare it with bo ལག  arm, sit-jap tɯ-jaʁ  arm and suggest that the comparisons are more compatible with an och - reconstruction such as *klˁak. | Alternatively, Schuessler (2007) reconstructs the och - minimally as *kâk < *klak and posits an zh aav origin, comparing it to mkh-mnc-pro *knlak  popliteal space; armpit, km ក្លៀក  armpit, both from mkh-pro *kʔik *kʔik ~ *kʔiək ~ *kʔaik armpit.

kanji/臣.content:
臣

Retainer, Subject


On: シン, ジン
Kun: —
Kyūjitai: 𢘑
Componentes: 臣


Etimología
In Old Chinese, nominalization with nasal suffix of the verb 視 to watch, hence literally “watcher; supervisor” (Schuessler 2007). In the archaic language of the Shang oracle bones (late second millennium BCE), this word referred to “royal officers, many of whose individual names were recorded, who served in the royal court, received the king’s orders to launch military expeditions and other tasks, and received royal gifts” (Keightley 2012).

Etimología
“Warship (with boards installed on its four sides to defend against arrow attacks)” (Shiming) > “warship” > “ship” (Guangya). A specialised character derived from 檻 fence, railing, board; see there for more on the external etymology. | This character is a classic example of historical misreadings of unfamiliar characters. The l- initial in southern dialects is probably due to confusion with 濫 to overflow, not due to divergent evolutions of the Old Chinese cluster initial *gr- as this character is often cited as an example of. Likewise, the readings in other Chinese are misreadings, although this is more subtle. Expected Mandarin reflex is xiàn, and jiàn is due to confusion with 鑑 mirror; to reflect. Wu and Eastern Min readings are results of confusion with zh 檻#Pronunciation_2. Despite these irregularities, all the Sinoxenic readings are regular. zh spelling pronunciations

Schuessler (2015) does not consider the bo - word to be cognate. | * Blench (2012) suggests that the Chinese word is borrowed from zh hmx-pro - and that the my - word may be a late loan from och -. | * STEDT reconstructs sit-pro *g/s-rwa  taro; yam; tuber, whence the bo - word. This etymon is regarded as allofamically related this word and 薯. | * Gong Hwang-cherng (2002) and Baxter and Sagart (2017) also suggest that this word is related to the bo - word.

Etimología
Unclear.  | Possibly of zh sit origin. Schuessler (2007) derives it from zh sit-pro *baːr  bloom, flower and thus an example of possible *b ~ *w variation, with final -r moved to medial position. If so, cognate with 葩; outside Sinitic languages Sinitic, compare my ပန်း, lep ᰓᰫᰲ, lus páar, etc. Sagart (2021) also connects it to 葩, modifying Baxter and Sagart’s (2014) reconstruction to *Cə-pʰˤra and proposing the sound changes *Cə-pʰ- > *Cə-ɸ- > *ɸ- > xw-. | Sagart & Baxter (2024) reconstruct 荂 ~ 葩 and 荂 ~ 花 (with unknown prefix *X turning labial stops into Middle Chinese fricative initials in  荂 ~ 花) (which might have already happened by the time of the Western Zhou dynasty, as shown by the presence of the 于 radical in its earliest form 𦻏). Furthermore, they propose cognacy to kar-pro *phɔᴬ  flower and reconstruct zh sit-pro *p(h)a  idem. Outside Sino-Tibetan, they propose cognacy to map-pro *pahpah  flower, petal; leaf. | Alternatively, from zh aav; compare aav-pro *bka(ː)ʔ  flower (Schuessler, 2007). | 華 to flower is a derivative.

On: ラク

Componentes: 艹, 洛


Etimología
From zh sit-pro *klaʔ  to fall (STEDT under PTB *(k/g)la-k/y/t, Schuessler, 2007): | :within Sinitic, cognate to 露 “dew”, 下 down, below, to descend, to fall down , 陊 “to collapse” and 阤 “hillside, slope”; | :outside of Sinitic, cognate to lus tla tla ~ tlâk and lus thla thla ~ thlâk, my ကျ  to fall and my ချ  to drop. | Schuessler attributes OC *r-, instead of expected **l-, to possible Austroasiatic influence: compare km < km. However, Matisoff (2003) identifies several ST etyma which display TB *(C‑)l- vs. OC *(C‑)r‑ correspondence (e.g. sit-pro *l(j)a(k/ŋ)  good, beautiful → 良, sit-pro *g/m-liŋ  neck → 領, etc.) and TB *(C‑)r- vs. OC *(C‑)l‑ (e.g. sit-pro *g-rjum  salt → 鹽); so irregularities in correspondence do not necessarily indicate foreign influences. | Contemporary southern usage possibly reinforced by a Kra-Dai term. The term has been associated with za loengx  to fall. | Zhengzhang Shangfang Zhengzhang suggested that Pronunciation 2 was a result of loss of final consonant of the retained Old Chinese Pronunciation 1.

kanji/蒜.content:
蒜

Garlic


On: サン
Kun: にんにく, ひる, のびる
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 艹, 祘


Etimología
Matisoff considers this to be derived from zh sit-pro *swa-n  garlic, but more likely this may be a plant imported from the Western Regions in the Qin Dynasty Qin–Han Dynasty Han era. The relatively late attestation and the earlier form of 卵蒜 attest to the latter theory. | Compare sa लशुन लशुन, pi lasuṇa, pi lasuna. The Old Chinese reconstruction was revised to a *-or rhyme in the Baxter–Sagart system, akin to its homophone *算 to calculate. Hence compare fa سیر  garlic, kho sārmā-  the plant Basella cordifolia or B. lucida or B. rubra, hu sárma  {{taxfmt Ornithogalum genus sp.}}, as well as tr sarımsak, mn саримс. | Either way this word is cognate with the second syllable of my ကြက်သွန်  onion, my ကြက်သွန်ဖြူ  garlic.

Etimología
zh. Various theories have been proposed: | * Starostin sets up zh sit-pro *lăj  snake, comparing this with lus hlai-ba  a species of snake and kac palai  a species of iguana. He also compares it to qfa-kms-pro *dzuːi²  snake. Schuessler (2007) considers these tbq forms to be unrelated. | * Matisoff (2003) relates it to zh sit-pro *s-b/m-ruːl  snake, but this comparison is no longer held in STEDT. | * Sagart (2005) relates it to tbq-lol-pro *lay¹/²  python, which STEDT derives from sit-pro *g-lja(ŋ/k)  python, as well as map-pro *bulay  snake. Comparison with the map form has been challenged by Orlandi (2018). | * Schuessler (2007) notes similarity to qfa-lic-pro *ljaːɦ  snake (from Pre-Hlai *Cilaːɦ) as well as to map words, such as rad ala  snake, but considers the qfa-tak forms to be possible borrowings from Chinese. (He does not seem to address the map forms directly.) In his view, a more likely relationship is with the /-lé/ in km រលេ  sinuously, in a twisting or wiggling manner (as a snake swimming). In Old Chinese, this also provides the second syllable in 委蛇 winding; compliant; graceful. zh 蛇  the winding thing is then a euphemism for common Sino-Tibetan 虺 snake for taboo reasons. | * Zhengzhang (2011) relates it to map-pro *Sulaʀ  snake.

The -ko may be the same as in 海鼠 こ, as both are soft-bodied marine organisms. Related terms could then be interpreted as 煎海鼠 いりこ ko eaten after being boiled and dried, 海鼠 なまこ ko still raw, 蛸 たこ many-armed ko. Speculatively, the -ko element may instead be a diminutive suffix, commonly written as 子 -こ, related to 小 こ.

Dissolve, Melt


On: ユウ

Kyūjitai: 螎
Componentes: 鬲, 虫


Etimología
“hot air; steam; heat” > “to melt” > “to blend”. | Sino-Tibetan; compare my လောင်  to burn; to be burnt; to scorch. Related to 蟲 hot; hot air; hot weather (as in 蟲蟲), 爞 hot weather and possibly the word family of *lVm: 焰 fire. | It belongs to a word family comprising characters meaning “to melt, to smelt, to fuse, to dissolve”. In modern times the various characters have taken on their specialised meanings: | * 融 to melt (at normal temperature); to blend | * 鎔 to smelt; to melt (at a high temperature) | * 熔 to smelt; to melt (at a high temperature) | * 溶 to dissolve (in a liquid)

From zh sit-pro *s-hjwəj-t  blood (STEDT; Schuessler, 2007). | Baxter and Sagart (2014) reconstruct the och - as und *m̥ˤik to account for word-family connections with 脈 vein, 衊 defiled blood as well as its use as a phonetic component in 侐 still; quiet, which is in the same word family as 宓 quiet; silent (Sagart, 1999b; Baxter and Sagart, 2017). Sagart (1999b) argues that this word is not genetically related to the tbq form with *s-hjw-, but that this word has been borrowed into tbq.  | Schuessler (2019) critiques Sagart (1999b)‘s proposal that Tibeto-Burman languages all over Southeast Asia and the Himalayas in early dynastic time would and could borrow Chinese words, and Baxter and Sagart (2014)‘s reconstruction 血 *m̥ˤik}} as resulting from “phonetic over-interpretation of graphs” and confusing etymological link with mental association between “blood” and “vein”.

Chinese has final -ŋ because initial and final m are mutually exclusive (Schuessler, 2003; Schuessler, 2007). | This word’s rare occurrence in a traditional saying indicates that it is not part of the active vocabulary of OC, but a | survival from a substrate language.

Etimología
From 牙 tooth: | : 近代 通 謂 府廷 為 公衙，公衙 即 古 之 公朝 也。字 本 作「牙」。《^詩》曰：「祈父 予 王 之 爪牙。」祈父，司馬，掌 武備，象 猛獸，以 爪牙 為 衛。故 軍 前 大 旗 謂 之「牙旗」，出師 則 有 建牙、禡牙 之 事，軍 中 聽 號令，必 至 牙旗 之 下，稱 與 府朝 無 異。近 俗 尚武，是 以 通 呼 公府 為 公牙，府門 為 牙門。字 稱 訛變，轉 而 為「衙」也。 In the recent era, the official court is commonly known as gongya (“official tooth”), which is gongchao (“official court”) in ancient times. The character is originally {{lang zh 牙. The Classic of Poetry says, “Qifu, we are the claws and teeth of the king.” Qifu is the minister of war, who is in charge of weaponry and, like a ferocious beast, defends using his claws and teeth. Hence the large banner before the army is known as the “tooth banner”; when sending the troops out, the tooth banner is erected and offered sacrifices; when listening to military orders, the army must be under the tooth banner; this is no different from the government office. In recent times, military affairs are commonly revered, so the gongfu is known as gongya and the fumen is known as yamen. The character has changed into zh 衙.|CL-L|ref=Tang dynasty, zh 封演 (Feng Yan), zh s:封氏聞見記/卷五 封氏聞見記 (Master Feng’s Records of Things Heard and Seen)|collapsed=y}}
