kanji/西.title: 西
kanji/西.content:
西

West, Spain


On: セイ, サイ, ス
Kun: にし
Kyūjitai: 㢴
Componentes: 一, 𠁤


Etimología
The word is traditionally reconstructed to have a /*s/-initial in Old Chinese, e.g. /*sɯːl/ in Zhengzhang (2003). However, recent scholarship has suggested that the Old Chinese initial should instead be reconstructed as /*s-nˤ/, one of the reasons being *西 appears to be the phonetic in 迺 nǎi, the archaic graphic variant of 乃. The new reconstruction, /*s-nˤər/ in Baxter and Sagart (2014), also accounts for how *西 can be the phonetic in 哂 to smile. For more information, see Sagart (2004), Baxter and Sagart (2014) and Nohara (2018). | In light of the new construction with the initial consonant cluster /*s-nˤ/, the possibilities of the etymology of zh 西, aside from being cognate with 棲 to roost; to rest (B-S OC /*s-nˤər/), include: | * Related to bo ནེར་བ  to sink; to fall gradually (Unger, 1990). | * Related to cdm नेलःसा  to go down; to sink, which may be the same etymon as the Written Tibetan word above (Schuessler, 2007). | * Related to the root 尼 nǐ to stop (OC /*nˤərʔ/ for intransitive form, /*nˤərʔ-s/ for transitive form in Baxter and Sagart (2014)). | * Related to bo མནལ  sleep and my နား  to rest; to stop for a while (Hill, 2019). | * An zh aav - nominal n-infix derivative from the root “go down”, as in omx cnis  ghat  Proto-Sinitic *sn-. If true, then this etymon literally means “the place where one goes down to” > Mon “ghat” > OC “nest, west” and its base form is 濟 via Austroasiatic (Schuessler, 2007).

Etimología
Earliest extant attestation is in Discourses of the States (translation adapted from Keightley, 1989): | * {{zh-x|古 者 民 神 不 雜。民 之 精爽 不 攜貳 者，而 又 能 齊 肅 衷 正，其 智 能 上下 比 義，其 聖 能 光 遠 宣 朗，其 明 能 光照 之，其 聰 能 聽 徹 之，如是 則 明神 降 之，在 男 曰 覡，在 女 曰 巫。是 使 制 神 之 處-位 次-主，而 為{wéi} 之 牲 器 時-服。|[I]n antiquity, the (officers in charge of the) people and the (officers in charge of the) spirits were not intermingled (i.e., were not mixed up). There were those among the people whose spiritual vigor was undiverted and who were also able to act in reverence and rectitude; their intelligence could conform to what is right in the upper and lower realms, their sagacity could blaze afar and display what is bright, their clear vision could illuminate it, their astute hearing could provide thorough understanding of it. Thus, the spirits (ming shen 明神) descended to them. In the case of men, (these special people) were called Xi 覡; in the case of women, they were called Wu 巫. Thus, one employed them to give order to the position and precedence of the spirits and to prepare their sacrificial victims, the ritual vessels, and the ceremonial garments of the seasons.|ref=Guoyu|collapsed=yes}}

The Tibeto-Burman *-ŋ final variant is reflected in 觥 drinking vessel made from animal horn (Schuessler, 2007). Possibly also related to 鹿 deer (Sagart, 1999). | A derivative is 餃 stuffed dumpling, named for its horn-like shape (Norman, 1988). | It is probably unrelated with ine-pro  *ḱr̥h₂nós ( < ine-pro *ḱerh₂-) and sem-pro *ḳarn- despite the phonological and semantic resemblance between the three.

Etimología

Starostin sets up zh sit-pro *k-lok  to recite; to give notice for this, and also includes my လျှောက်  to tell; to ask; to petition; word-for-word translation; indiscriminately and lus thlûk  accent, tone, intonation. Related to 讟 resentment, slander < to grumble; complaint. | STEDT provisionally sets up zh sit-pro *s-g-(l/r)əwk  to read, relating it to 牘 tablet. | Sagart (1999) argues that “read” cannot be the primary meaning, since existence of the concept “to read” before the invention of writing is questionable. There was likely no writing at the time of the split between Chinese and other Sino-Tibetan languages, therefore the Tibetan word may represent a borrowing from Chinese.

Possibly from zh sit-pro *C-pək  pig; if so, cognate with bo ཕག, my ဝက် (Benedict, 1972; STEDT). | However, there are phonological mismatches: | * A medial *-r- in och - should correspond to a pre-initial in tbq -, but this is not present (Schuessler, 2007). | * A final *-k is present in tbq - yet absent in och -, which is an irregular correspondence (Schuessler, 2007; Sagart, 2011b). | Alternatively, Schuessler (2007) considers Waic languages Waic und *bras  wild boar a better match. kanji/象.title: 象
kanji/象.content:
象

Elephant, Pattern After, Imitate, Image, Shape, Sign (of The Times)


On: ショウ, ゾウ
Kun: かたど.る
Kyūjitai: 𧰼
Componentes: 𠂊, 𫩏, 𧰨


Etimología
This character is used to represent two semantic fields ‘elephant; tusk’ and ‘to outline; to depict; to delineate; to represent; to resemble; to map’. Both fields are found from the earliest layers of the edited literature onwards, whereas only the first meaning is amply attested in oracle bone inscriptions. | Traditionally, the two senses are treated as related, with the sense of ‘to depict; to resemble’ considered a derivative of the sense of ‘elephant’. The derivation from the ‘elephant’ meaning to the ‘likeness’ meaning is explained in Han Feizi, c 221 BCE: “Men rarely see living elephants. As they come by the skeleton of a dead elephant, they imagine its living form according to its features. Therefore it comes to pass that whatever people use for imagining the real is called zh 象 (Chinese Mandarin XIANG).” | Modern etymology studies on Old Chinese have challenged this opinion. | As for the ‘elephant; tusk’ sense, this is a widely used area word in East and Southeast Asia. Literature opinions differ on the origin and immediate relationship of this Chinese word; some (e.g. Schuessler, 2007) believe the Chinese form is a loanword from a Southern language, since it is unlikely that peoples all over Southeast Asia and the Himalayan foothills would borrow a word from Northern China to denote an indigenous animal. Others believe the direction of borrowing is reversed (i.e. Tai-Kadai borrowing from Chinese), and that Chinese zh 象 should be compared with bo གླང, bo གླང་ཆེན  elephant arising from a common zh sit-pro *glaŋ  ox, bull; elephant, which may ultimately have an zh aav - origin (Schuessler, 1994 (unpublished) apud Behr, 2004a; cf. omx draṅ, omx, mnw ဂြၚ်  horn, tusk and khr from aav-pro *krɨŋ  horn). The second viewpoint is supported by the early attestation of this character and the archaeological findings of the historical ranges of elephants. However, Schuessler disputes that second viewpoint and links ST *glaŋ to 犅 ox, bull. | See below for a tentative borrowing history of the various forms of this general area word.

On: バイ

Possibly from zh sit-pro *laj (PTB *g/m/s-lay ~ r/s-ley ~ b-rey); compare kar-pro *breᴬ  to buy, tbq-bdg-pro *prai¹  to buy, bo རྗེ  to exchange; to barter (Schuessler, 2007; Sagart, 1999, 2011). Benedict (1967, 1972) considers this allofam to be a result of borrowing from Austro-Tai languages Austro-Tai und *(m)baḷi several times into Sino-Tibetan languages. | Alternatively, Haudricourt and Strecker (1991) consider zh 買 and zh 賣 to be borrowed from zh hmx, which may have a family of verbs related to possession: hmx-pro *mɛjX  to buy zh 買}}, hmx-pro *mɛjH  to buy zh 賣}}, hmx-pro *ʔ-mɛj  to grasp, hmx-pro *n-mɛj  to have (Ratliff, 2010). However, Sagart (1995) argues that the direction of borrowing is more likely to be from Chinese to Hmong-Mien because Hmong-Mien does not seem to have a suffix that would give rise to the tone in the word for “to buy”. In addition to these two ways of relating the Chinese word to Hmong-Mien, Ratliff (2010) proposes common inheritance as a third option and maintains that more evidence is needed to determine which of the three explanations are correct. | The surname only appears among Taiwanese aboriginals and Hui people in Mainland China. The surname is from the Siraya name Takalomay in Taiwan or possibly from the name zh 買買提 for Hui people.

Etimología
thumb|zh 鉞 戉 or zh 鉞: large battle-axe used as a symbol of authority in ancient China. | ; “to go over; to surpass; to overstep; to turn” | : From zh sit-pro *ɢʷrat  to travel; to go through. | : Related to 𨒋 to go over, 䟠 to go beyond; to transgress (Wang, 1982) and perhaps 于 to go (Schuessler, 2007). | ; “modal particle” | : Related to 曰, 于 and 粵 (Wang, 1982). | ; “Yue; Viet; State of Yue” | : Related to 粵 Yue; Cantonese. | : This is a general name for numerous indigenous tribes in ancient southern China, which are collectively called Baiyue. The ancient State of Yue during the Zhou dynasty of China was initially written as 戉 large battle-axe — alternatively written as *𫑛 — and it is commonly believed the name Yue originates from this instrument, which was widely found in neolithic cultures of southeastern China and served as a symbol of authority and royalty. | : See 戉 for more on the etymology.

Car


On: シャ
Kun: くるま
Kyūjitai: 𠦴
Componentes: 車


Etimología
zh :bor ine-toc-pro:*kuk(ä)le | Perhaps a loan from an zh ine language because the horse and chariot were introduced into China around 1200 BC from Inner Asia; compare xto kukäl, txb kokale  wagon; cart (Mair, 1990, Bauer, 1994), from zh ine-toc-pro *kuk(ä)le, from zh ine-pro *kʷékʷlos, from a reduplication of the root ine-pro *kʷel-  to turn. Cognate with en wheel, grc κύκλος, lt kaklas  neck, etc. | Sagart and Baxter (2025) specifically pinpoint descent from some reflex of zh iir-pro *čakrám and update their 2014 reconstructions to *t.[qʰ]rA > chē and *[C.q]ra > jū. They also suppose that the variation of pronunciations could be attributed to separate borrowing events from Indo-Aryan and Iranian. | An older variant survives in Mandarin 軲轆 wheel (Bauer, 1994). Alternatively, the word is a derivation by k-prefix from 舁 to lift (Baxter and Sagart, 1998); compare the semantic parallel in bo ཐེག་པ  vehicle; carriage (<to support; to carry; to lift).zh doublets | Pronunciations 1 and 2 are cognate. A similar phonological doublet is 處 and 居 (Schuessler, 2007). Pronunciation 2 is traditionally regarded as the older pronunciation. | The sense of lewd content is derived from zh 老司機.

kanji/辰.title: 辰
kanji/辰.content:
辰

Sign Of The Dragon, 7-9am, Fifth Sign Of Chinese Zodiac, Shin Dragon Radical (no. 161)


On: シン, ジン
Kun: たつ
Kyūjitai: 𫝕
Componentes: 厂, 二, 𠄌, 乀, 丿


Etimología
; “to vibrate” | : Related to 震 to shake and 振 to excite, from zh sit-pro *dar ~ d(u/i)r  to tremble; to shiver (Schuessler, 2007). | ; “fifth earthly branch” | : Norman (1985) suggests that it is from zh aav; compare aav-pro *tlan  python, whence vi trăn, km ថ្លាន់, mnw ကၠန်. However, Ferlus (2013) points to reconstructions like *dər (Baxter & Sagart) and *ᴸdzɨr (Ferlus) and remarks that those do not match any animal’s name in Mainland Southeast Asia linguistic area Mainland Southeast Asian (MSEA) languages. Therefore, zh 辰 might have been associated arbitrarily with the dragon (*龍). | :Smith (2011) agrees with the proposal (e.g. by Guo, 1931) that 辰 initially depicted an agricultural implement made from clams’ shells and was the original form of 蜃 mollusc, clam; so he proposes that the fifth earthly branch depicted the moon’s second waning-gibbous phase, which looks like a clam. He also suggests that 辰 also represented the ovoid-shaped rising sun and is thus related to 晨 early morning. | ; “time” | : From 時 time + nominalizing suffix -n, literally “that which is proceeding” (Schuessler, 2007). This word partially converges with 晨 morning (ibid.). | ; “heavenly body” | : The endopassive of 振 to shake; to stir, literally “to stir oneself”, i.e. “when life begins to stir” > “heavenly bodies that mark time” (ibid.).

On: ユウ
Kun: とり
Kyūjitai: 丣
Componentes: 酉


Etimología
;“wine; wine vessel” | : From zh sit-pro *jəw  liquor (STEDT); cognate with 酒 wine. | ; “tenth earthly branch” | : Smith (2011) suggests that this branch denoted the “waxing half-moon”, “construed as a vessel filling with liquid”. Noting Schuessler (2007)‘s observation that 酉’s OC pronunciation started with *r-, Smith reconstructs *r-juʔ which would later lost its archaic pre-initial *r-, the same phonological split seen in pairs like 游 ~ 遊 to flow, to roam > yóu vs. 流 flow > liú. Smith further supposes that *r-juʔ, is an endoactive derivative of *r-ju “flow” by the suffix *-ʔ, meaning “the flowing stage”. | : As for 酉’s association with the chicken, Norman (1985) proposes that Chinese and Thai forms derived from Viet-Muong *rə̆k ~ *ruk, truncated from mkh-vie-pro *r-kaː  chicken, yet Ferlus (2013) thinks this correspondence unlikely. Possibly, 酉 was arbitrarily associated with the chicken, just like 辰 with the dragon. | ;“unitary” | :From zh en unitary unitary.

Various etymologies have been proposed: | * From a hypothetical common Sino-Tibetan *la (“area far from settlements; wilderness”): compare bo ལ  mountain pass; hillside; mountainslope (Schuessler, 2007); | * Related to mkh-pro *laʔ  to spread, extend: compare km លា  to unfold, spread, open out (Schuessler, 2007); | * From a Sino-Tibetan root meaning “hut; pantry”: compare bo ལྷས  pen; fold; cattle enclosure (Starostin).

kanji/鏡.title: 鏡
kanji/鏡.content:
鏡

Mirror, Speculum, Barrel-head, Round Rice-cake Offering


On: キョウ, ケイ
Kun: かがみ
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 金, 竟


Etimología
Probably cognate with 景 bright, 影 shadow (Wang, 1982; Schuessler, 2007; Baxter and Sagart, 2014). Gong (2019) identifies the unknown preinitial *C in the reconstruction *C.qraŋʔ-s by Baxter and Sagart (2014) with *s based on evidence from Old Vietnamese, and further posits that it is an instrumental noun derived by prefixation of *s- to the verb 映 to reflect, which is itself a denominal derived from 影 shadow; image; however, Gong acknowledges that his emendation of *C.qraŋʔ-s to *s.qraŋʔ-s is incompatible with Reconstructions of Old Chinese#Baxter–Sagart (2014) Baxter & Sagart’s 2014 system, as *s.qraŋʔ-s would have become Middle Chinese *tsrjaeŋH instead of *kjaeŋH (ibid.). | Alternatively, it may be derived from 亮 to shine with the nominalising *k- prefix (Schuessler, 2007; apud Baxter, p.c.). | STEDT compares zh 鏡, zh 景 and zh 亮, among others, to tbq-kuk-pro *klaaŋ-I, tbq-kuk-pro *klaan-II  to shine; light; bright. | This word is relatively late and is perhaps re-etymologized from the nearly identical earlier word 監, 鑑 mirror (Schuessler, 2007), which Wang (1982) treats as cognate. Gong (2019) considers zh 鏡 to be an unrelated neologism replacing zh 鑑.

On: チョウ
Kun: なが.い, おさ
Kyūjitai: 镸
Componentes: 一, 𠄌, 乀, 丿


Etimología
Three pronunciations below are cognate, all derived from the original root of zh 張. | Pronunciation 1 (“long”) is the endopassive derivative (“be extended, be stretched”), with intransitive voicing. The lack of Tibeto-Burman cognates with the same meaning indicate that this is a Chinese innovation. Pronunciation 2 (“to grow”) is the endoactive derivative. The different pronunciations are one of the few instances of contemporary grammatical tone in Mandarin. | See zh 張 for more.

Unclear. Schuessler (2007) proposes several possibilities: | * From zh aav; compare km ភ្លៀង  rain, from mkh-pro *(p)liɲ ~ *(p)liəɲ ~ (p)liiɲ  sky, rain. | * Possibly related to kac marang  rain, for which STEDT sets up zh sit-pro *m/s-raŋ  rain. Starostin also relates it to this Jingpho word and sets up zh sit-pro  *rēŋ to drop, also comparing bo སྤྲིན  cloud and my ရည်  liquid; juice. | * Possibly related to 隕 to drop and 霣 to rain; to fall down like rain if one assumes zh sit-pro *r/s/g-wa  water; rain (or its variant sit-pro  *rwe-) can be simplified to *re- and *we-. | The character was later repurposed in 1248 by mathematician Li Ye as a placeholder, extending from its a little bit (of rain) meaning to indicate a bit more remaining. In Li Ye’s notation, a number like 302 would be represented as zh 三zh 百zh 零zh 二, literally three hundred and remaining two, with the zh 零 character used as a means of skipping the tens place, by indicating zero tens. It would thus implicitly take on the meaning of en zero.

However, Schuessler (2007) notes that och 豆 seems like a tone C (zh 去聲) derivation from och 頭, which may have originally meant “skull”. | * Baxter and Sagart (2014) reconstructs the Old Chinese with a *m- prefix for human body parts, deriving it from och 兜  helmet; hood.

kanji/風.content:
風

On: フウ, フ
Kun: かぜ, かざ-, -かぜ
Kyūjitai: 凨
Componentes: 几, 䖝


Etimología
Possibly from zh sit-pro *buŋ  wind (STEDT). Velar nasal final -ŋ, restored later in Middle Chinese (Schuessler, 2007), is preserved in cognates like Proto-Central Naga *m-puŋ, kac mabung, kac nbung, duu nvmbeung. | Pronunciations 1, 2, and 3 are all cognates; with both 2 and 3 evolving from *prəm-s, exoactive (with causative suffix -s) of *prəm (Schuessler, 2007). It is unclear how Old Chinese *prəm is related to bo རླུང and tai-pro *C̬.lɯmᴬ. | ko 바람 may have been borrowed from Chinese (Zhao, 2007). The Chinese word has a wide range of extended meanings, and interestingly many of these have exact parallels in the Korean item. Compare Chinese zh 風流 and zh 風騷 with Korean ko 바람둥이. | Cognate with: | * 飛廉 | * 蜚蠊 (note the preservation of the -r- infix in Old Chinese through disyllabification, also 嵐, 葻) | * 瘋 | * 諷 | * 帆 | The development from Old Chinese to Middle Chinese was irregular, driven by dissimilation of the initial and coda bilabial consonants.

kanji/馬.title: 馬
kanji/馬.content:
馬

Horse


On: バ
Kun: うま, うま-, ま
Kyūjitai: 𫠉
Componentes: 灬


Etimología
zh:,yue:,gan:,hak:mâ,cdo:mā,nan:bé,wuu:马 | Wanderwort (Jacques, 2009; Felner and Hill, 2019; Lai et al., 2020). This word is often compared to other sit forms, e.g., bo རྨང, my မြင်း, sit-jap mbro, txg 𘆝, cdm, tbq-kuk-pro *raŋ (> cnh ràŋ) (Benedict, 1972; Schuessler, 2007; STEDT), but the lack of nasal coda in Chinese would be irregular, suggesting borrowing from a sister language rather than common ancestry (Sagart et al., 2019). Outside of sit, this has also been compared to mn ᠮᠣᠷᠢ, ko 말, ja - 馬 うま (Schuessler, 2007; Lai et al., 2020). | The sense of “big” is derived from “horse”; compare the English uses of en horse. For the insect prefix sense, see zh 螞. It has converged with the sense of “big”. | The surname is popularly known to be prevalent among Hui Muslims, where it is likely derived from zh ar مُحَمَّد, although the surname zh 馬 itself predates him.

On: キ
Kun: —
Kyūjitai: 𮪍
Componentes: 馬, 奇


Etimología
Wanderwort in the E/SE Asian Sprachbund. The STEDT reconstructs sit-pro *gi  to ride; to sit astride; to sit (horse), and comments that “many of the TB forms seem to be borrowings from Chinese zh 騎”. | Outside Sino-Tibetan, cognates are also found in Hmong-Mien, Tai-Kadai and some Mon-Khmer languages. Benedict (1975) surmises that this is an ancient loan into Proto-Sino-Tibetan from Austro-Tai: | … but these [Tibeto-Burman] forms appear to involve old loans from AT [Austro-Tai] with typical loss of an original medial *w (Thai *khwi ~ *gwi). | while Peiros (1998), Sagart (2006), Schuessler (2007) (who suggests that 騎 to ride is possibly endopassive “let oneself be carried (on the back of an animal)” of 荷 to carry) and Pittayaporn (2014) think the directionality of borrowing is reversed. The following excerpt is taken from Sagart’s review (2006) of Matisoff’s book Handbook of Proto-Tibeto-Burman (2003): | The collection of forms under Matisoff’s high-vowelled *gyi ‘ride’ are from TB languages in contact with Chinese (Lolo-Burmese, Qiangic, Tujia): they are best regarded as late loans from Chinese. … The idea that the Chinese vocabulary of agriculture, metallurgy, horse-riding etc. might contain numerous loans from an early SEA language is simply not to be taken seriously in view of modern Asian archaeology (Bellwood 1997), quite apart from the fact that it makes no linguistic sense (Sagart 1999 for metal names). Yet Matisoff’s book is scattered with observations telling the reader that words like ‘writing brush’ and ‘ride’ just discussed may well be loans from Austro-Tai into ST (188; 504). | Below lists some cognates for “to ride” found in various languages in this Sprachbund. | * Lolo-Burmese: tbq-lob-pro *gyi ~ dzyi: my စီး, ii ꋩ, ii ꊪ | * Southwestern Tai: *kʰwiːᴮ: th ขี่, lo ຂີ່, za gwih | * Hmong-Mien: hmx-pro *ɟej: mww caij | * Mon-Khmer: West Bahnaric *ɟih, km ជិះ, vi cưỡi | Also compare map-pro *sakay  catch a ride, join a group, ride on something. | Pronunciation 2 is a Late Old Chinese general purpose derivation from Pronunciation 1 (Schuessler, 2007).

kanji/鮎.title: 鮎
kanji/鮎.content:
鮎

Freshwater Trout, Smelt


On: デン, ネン
Kun: あゆ, なまず
Kyūjitai: 鯰
Componentes: 魚, 占


Etimología
ja:鮎 | Ayu | thumb|250px|ja 鮎 (ayu, ai): ayu or sweetfish. | あゆ | From ja ojp - of uncertain derivation. | * One commonly encountered etymology suggests that ayu may derive from ja 饗  hosting someone to a meal, in reference to the way that this fish may be used in Shinto offerings. the word ayu in reference to the fish appeared in the Nihon Shoki (720 ), and is thus too old for this shift to have occurred. | * Another common etymology states that ayu may be from extinct Old Japanese term ja 落ゆ  to fall, as nuts from a tree; to flow down, as liquid in a stream, in reference to the way that ayu swim downstream to spawn in the autumn. Some references suggest that this is not very eventful and that this etymology is therefore unlikely. However, there are terms specific to the ayu downstream migration, such as ja 落鮎  ayu migrating downstream to spawn and ja 鮎落つ  ayu migrating downstream to spawn, suggesting that this event has been culturally important enough that the ja  落ゆ derivation may be plausible. | * Alternatively, this term may be borrowed from ja ain アイ  arrow in reference to how fast the fish moves. See also obsolete Japanese reading ai below. | The kanji spelling  鮎 in reference to sweetfish is specific to Japan, probably in reference to the way the fish (魚) stakes out its territory (占). There is another tale wherein Empress Jingū caught an ayu and thereby prophesied (also spelled  占) the outcome of a battle, but this is likely a folk etymology. In China and elsewhere, the  鮎 character refers instead to catfish. | The kanji spelling 年魚 is in reference to the common one-year lifespan of this fish. | The kanji spelling 香魚 is in reference to its sweet-tasting flesh.

Sushi, Seasoned Rice


On: シ, キ

Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 魚, 旨


Etimología
According to the Hànyǔ Tóngyuán Cí Dàdiǎn (zh 漢語同源詞大典), this reading belongs to an Old Chinese word family centred on the concept of “smallness” or “finely divided things”. It is cognate with 鴲 small finch and 柴 twigs, fine wood. The semantic core—reducing an object into minute pieces—perfectly aligns with the classical definition of minced meat.

Etimología
かつお | ja:カツオ | Skipjack tuna | thumb | From ja ojp - katuwo.  Found in the Man’yōshū of 759. | /katuwo/ → /kat͡suwo/ → /kat͡suo/ | Two possible derivations: | * A shift from a compound of ja 堅 魚, from the long-standing practice of drying lower-grade tuna into hard blocks, in part due to the common presence of parasites. A folk etymology also derives this kanji character, compare 木工 → ja 杢  woodworker and 麻呂 → ja 麿. | * A shift from a compound of ja 勝つ 魚. | Considering the rules of Old Japanese phonology, specifically that two vowels are not allowed in sequence, resulting in elision or fusion, the kata + uo → katuo shift seems likely.  This derivation may be partially corroborated by the rare historical synonym ja 堅魚, literally “hard fish”. | The kanji spelling is an example of 国%訓 こっ%くん Japanese-specific kun’yomi and its use may stem from the 堅魚 spelling.

kanji/鱷.title: 鱷
kanji/鱷.content:
鱷

Crocodile, Alligator


On: ガク
Kun: わに
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 魚, 噩


Etimología
Within Chinese, Carr (1990) relates it to: | * 咢 to beat the drum, either because drumming was associated with dragons or because some drums were made of crocodilian skins (Schuessler, 2007). | * Words for “fear”, e.g. 愕 startled; terrified, 噩 frightening; startling. | Outside of Chinese, Carr (1990) also relates it to: | * tai-pro  *ŋwak mythical water creature (reconstruction from Chamberlain, 1977), which Pittayaporn (2009-2010), reconstructing the root as tai-pro *ŋɯəkᴰ  crocodile, holds to be a loan from Chinese. | * Proto-Austro-Tai und *(m)baŋiwak  shark; crocodile, posited by Paul K. Benedict and proposed by him to give rise to the Tai word, as well as ja - 鰐 わに crocodilian; shark, 魚 うお fish. | Vovin (2021) notes that 鱷 “aquatic reptile, saltwater crocodile” was attested late, for the first time in Shuowen as *𧊜; and that “it would be very weird if the word for a ‘saltwater crocodile’ from the middle of Huang-he (黃河) river basin that lies quite far away from both tropics and the sea would be borrowed by Tai languages in Southern China”. Therefore, Vovin contends that, instead, 鱷 had been borrowed into Later Han Chinese from zh tai.

kanji/鳥.title: 鳥
kanji/鳥.content:
鳥

Bird, Chicken


On: チョウ
Kun: とり
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 灬


Etimología
Originally pronounced with a /t-/ initial (compare 島 island). In many dialects, it changed to a /n-/ initial to avoid homophony with the vulgar word 屌 penis, which may ultimately have developed from the sense “bird”. Birds/fowl are characteristically associated with Chinese slang for male genitalia; compare *雀 sparrow > penis and *雞 chicken > penis. | Alternatively, Schuessler (2007) hypothesised that the /n-/ initial form for “bird” may be unrelated to the /t-/ form. Instead, it may be connected with the Tai-Kadai word for bird; compare tai-pro *C̬.nokᴰ  bird, whence th นก. | The /t-/ form may be derived from zh sit-pro *daw  bird, cognate with kar-pro *thoᴮ  bird and tbq-bdg-pro *tao²  bird. | * rating in {{w Maimai (video game series)}} | : zh ja 鳥, from ja トリプルエス (triple S).

kanji/麗.title: 麗
kanji/麗.content:

Lovely, Beautiful, Graceful, Resplendent


On: レイ
Kun: うるわ.しい, うら.らか
Kyūjitai: 𠀙
Componentes: 丽, 鹿


Etimología
Schuessler (2007) minimally reconstructed this word’s OC pronunciation as *rêh and considered it a possible allofam of 麗 “number” < “what is calculated”, exopassive derivative of 歷 “to calculate”. | zh 麗 underwent this historical semantic shift: from “a pair” (Rites of Zhou Zhouli), to “mate, companion” (*儷) (Zuozhuan Zuo), to “paired”, to “well-proportioned” (Book of Rites Liji), and finally to “elegant, beautiful” (Chu Ci Chuci) as well as “refinement” (Book of Documents Shu).

kanji/鼻.title: 鼻
kanji/鼻.content:
鼻

Nose, Snout


On: ビ
Kun: はな
Kyūjitai: None
Componentes: 自, 畀


Etimología
From zh sit-pro *bi  nose; compare ii ꅳꁖ ꅳꁖ nose; snot. | Alternatively, it may be from zh sit-pro *s-brit  sneeze; nose; swallow, whence bo སྦྲིད  sneeze, but there is no trace of r in Chinese (Schuessler, 2007). | In some modern lects, including Mandarin, Gan, Jin, Wu, and Xiang, and even in the literary layer of some Min dialects, the word reflects a form with final *-t. For example, in standard Mandarin, the word is pronounced bí (implying an old entering tone) instead of bì (the expected reflex from the departing tone in Middle Chinese). This is due to a phonological phenomenon in the northwest, either an early loss of *-s in the *-ts cluster before regular final cluster simplification occurred (Baxter, 1992), or a dialectal change from *-s to *-t (Pulleybank, 1998).

ja:ホッケ | Okhotsk atka mackerel | thumb|250px|ja 𩸽 (hokke): an Arabesque greenling / Okhotsk atka mackerel in a tank. | ほっけ | ja. Various possibilities. | * According to legend, the first Japanese person to catch this fish was Buddhist monk Nichiji in the late 1290s, and he named it hokke after the ja 法華  Lotus Sutra. | * May be a shortening of ja ain - ain トドホッケ  sea lions lie down, the original Ainu name of 椴法華村 (Todohokke Mura, “Todohokke Village”), a village on the coast of Hokkaido where legend tells that Nichiji first caught this fish. | * May be a borrowing from ja ain - ain ホッケ  to lie down, possibly from the way that the fish sometimes appears to be lying on the bottom. | Considering that the fish is native to the waters off northern Japan where the Ainu were once prevalent, an Ainu derivation seems most likely.
